articles.title: India’s New Eye in the Sky: EOS-05 Satellite and What It Means for South Asia
articles.full_text:
EOS-05 is a single satellite that is part of a broader imitative of India to strengthen its ISR capabilities.
The Indian Space Research Organization (ISRO) recently launched a new surveillance satellite designated as EOS-05 into geosynchronous earth orbit (GEO). The launch was carried out with the GSLV-F17 rocket.
The satellite – launched on September 4 – is the first earth observation satellite deployed in GEO by India. The satellite will allow New Delhi to continuously observe the subcontinent from an altitude ranging between 34,903 km and 35,884 km. The chairman of ISRO, V. Narayanan, said that “EOS-05 will become India’s first dedicated imaging satellite from the geo orbit providing important strategic data for the country.” 
The launch of the satellite is part of India’s long-term plan to strengthen its intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) capabilities. The satellite will provide India with the capability to persistently track military movements in the subcontinent – especially Pakistan’s naval warships, aircraft, strategic assets movements, and force mobilization during crisis time. A new eye in the sky is an important military asset for India and can increase its counterforce capabilities in the age of emerging and disruptive technologies. 
India’s current space architecture consists of navigation, communication, ISR, and scientific satellites. For the purpose of communication, India has three dedicated military satellites – two of which are used by the Indian Navy and one by the Indian Air Force. Besides this, India has around 10 satellites that are dual-capable and can be used for military communication. The Indian navigation satellitessystem – known as Navigation with Indian Constellation (NavIC) – has three operational satellites, IRNSS-1B, IRNSS-1I , and NVS-01. However, for basic positioning service four satellites are required in orbit ; the next satellite NVS-03 would be launched soon. The Indian ISR architecture consists of the CROSAT series for Optical purposes, the RISAT and NISAR series for SAR purposes, and the EMISAT satellite for Electronic ISR. The newly launched EOS-05 would be India’s first ISR satellite that would give real-time persistent observation of the subcontinent. 
In 2024, India’s Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS) approved the Space Based Surveillance Phase-III (SBS-III) program that aimed to deploy 52 defense satellites into low-earth orbit (LEO) and geostationary orbit for surveillance. Under this project, ISRO will deploy 21 satellites and the private sector will develop 31 satellites. 
After the May 2025 crisis, there have been calls within the Indian strategic community to further strengthen Indian military capabilities in the space domain. For example, former Indian Chief of Defense Staff General Anil Chauhan, speaking at the Indian Defense Space Symposium (IDS) 2026, stressed the importance of military space based assets. He said, “If we fail in space, we will be forced to fight blind. However, if we dominate in space, we will fight with foresight.” 
The statement reflects a transformation in India’s strategic thinking vis-à-vis the military utility of space. The evolving character of warfare necessitates strengthening ISR architecture for maintaining persistent surveillance of strategically important areas both during peacetime and crisis situations. 
The newly launched EOS-05 satellite is particularly important as it adds to the persistent surveillance layer of India’s existing ISR architecture. Currently, India’s satellites are mainly in LEO, where they provide high-resolution imagery but have limitations because of rapid movement across the earth’s surface. EOS-05 being in geosynchronous orbit will provide prolonged observation of the subcontinent. This capability will strengthen India’s precision-strike capacity, as precision-strike missiles not only depend on range and accuracy but also timely information regarding the location of targets. Thus, in the broader sensor-to-shooter chain of network-centric warfare, space-based surveillance would play an important role. 
Moreover, persistent eyes in the sky can also strengthen India’s counterforce capabilities for both conventional and strategic purposes. For Pakistan, the implications of India strengthening ISR architecture and enhanced counterforce capabilities are direct. A persistent Indian eye in the sky would give its tri-services a near real-time picture of Pakistani naval deployments in the Arabian Sea, aircraft movements, and the dispersal of mobile missile launchers. As the survivability of mobile systems rests largely on their concealment, continuous wide-area surveillance, combined with high-resolution follow-up, shortens the time between detecting a target and striking it. India’s growing arsenal of long-range precision-strike missiles may become far more threatening with an added eye in space. 
Moreover, there are also benefits to India of the new satellite system for defensive purposes. It can also help India be better prepared for a counterstrike by Pakistan, especially with an advanced missile defense system. Having persistent capability to monitor movements of Pakistan’s troops, India can be more prepared to defend itself. 
However, this can have implications for South Asian deterrence dynamics. Faster detection, enhanced targeting information, and better precision-strike capabilities would lead to a compression of decision-making timelines during crisis. Because of territorial contiguity between India and Pakistan, decision-making timelines are already very short. Thus, increasing vulnerability of strategic assets to detection can induce Pakistan to early dispersal, mobilization, and further concealment of its military assets. This can also create a “use-it-or-lose-it dilemma” and further increases the risks of miscalculation and inadvertent escalation. Thus, enhanced space-based ISR capabilities can help in increasing situational awareness but would present new challenges for crisis stability and escalation management in South Asia.
In conclusion, EOS-05 is a single satellite that is part of a broader imitative of India to strengthen its ISR capabilities under the SBS-III program. However, its launching points toward an Indian strategic shift from periodic snapshots to persistent watch, and this enhancement of capability can have implications on how the next crisis between India and Pakistan will unfold. Islamabad has to further strengthen survivability of its conventional and strategic assets through concealment, deception, and mobility practices.

articles.title: Abroad, India’s RSS Speaks of ‘Love.’ At Home, Its Affiliates Attack Christians.
articles.full_text:
From church vandalism to grave desecration, assaults against Christian minorities are increasing in the large state of West Bengal since the BJP, an RSS offshoot, came to power in May.
Screenshot of a Facebook livestream shows the altercation at Goutam Bera’s residence in Ranichak village, West Bengal, Aug. 26, 2026.
Sutahata is a rural place in the eastern Indian state of West Bengal, which has been ruled by Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) since the May 2026 state elections. There, on August 26, about 50 people gathered at Goutam Bera’s residence in Ranichak village. It was a house fellowship gathering that involved Bible study and prayer. Many attendees were Hindus, mostly friends and acquaintances of the Bera family.
The news of the gathering reached members of Hindu supremacist organizations. One of them broadcast a live video on Facebook while on his way to Bera’s place. They had heard a Christian priest had gone there to convert Hindus. “Let’s see what they are up to,” he said. By the time the livestreamer reached Bera’s house, some of his fellows were already there. They barged into the house, abused those present and threw people out, before allegedly manhandling the rest of the attendees.
“You are Hindus. You have idols of Hindu deities at home. How could you bring in a Father and practice Christianity?” one can be heard shouting. “They have started this Jesus business now. See, we have recovered a Bible! My God, they have a Bible here!” 
One video shows the intruders – carrying saffron flags – ordering the prayer attendees, rather rudely and loudly, to chant “Hare Krishna, Hare Ram” and “Jai Shree Ram.” Another video shows the cops taking the prayer attendees to a police vehicle. At one point, people from the crowd can be heard shouting: “Thrash them, thrash them!” 
According to Joy Kumar Ghughu, the pastor who was reading from the Bible, the police first took 17 prayer attendees, including him, to the Sutahata block primary health center for treatment and a medical check-up. They were then taken to the Sutahata police station, where everyone was interrogated about the intention behind the gathering. Their mobile phones were examined. At about 8 p.m., they were told they could go. 
“We did not lodge any police complaint against the attackers because Jesus teaches forgiveness. We will pray for their well-being,” Ghughu told The Diplomat. 
He, however, asked why propagating Christianity should be objected to, when Article 25 of the Indian Constitution says that all persons are equally entitled to freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practice and propagate their religion freely. “We are not paying anyone to become Christians,” Ghughu said. 
Senior BJP leader Amit Malviya described the incident, along with two others, as “isolated local objections to prayer gatherings… peacefully resolved by the police.” However, videos posted on social media platforms by those involved in the attack tell a different story.  
The intruders identified themselves as members of Shree Ram Janmotsab Samity (Lord Ram birthday celebration committee). The Samity does not hide its links to the RSS, the BJP’s ideological and organizational parent. Its Facebook page regularly posts invites to events of the RSS and its affiliates, like the Vishwa Hindu Parishad (VHP). 
At Sutahata, a person recording on the spot identified himself and his fellows as belonging to the VHP. Showing videos of the organizers of the prayer gathering and the pastor present there, one of them told the video’s audience: “Beat them up with brooms whenever and wherever you see them. They are worse than terrorists.” 
In another video from the incident, uploaded to a Facebook page of Bajrang Dal, the youth wing of the VHP, the intruders said: “We are from VHP Chaitanyapur unit… Sanatan Dharma is the world’s greatest religion. Whenever you spot people we identified in our videos, just inform us.” The Hindu supremacists usually refer to Hinduism as Sanatan Dharma (eternal religion). 
A few hours later, in a Facebook post, the Samity said, “Let this serve as a warning to those who spread religious propaganda under the guise of ‘God the Father’: if we catch you, you will face severe consequences.”
Its based on actions like these that a recent database described the RSS family of organizations, popularly called the Sangh Parivar, as “the largest far-right network in history.” 
Modi called the RSS the world’s largest NGO (non-governmental organization).
That discrepancy gets to the heart of the RSS’s attempt to paint a very different picture of itself abroad.
Hindu civilizational identity rests on the idea that diversity and unity can coexist, RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat said in London at the beginning of September. “We must never lose sight of the fact that we are one.”
During a September 6 event in London as part of a U.S.-Canada-U.K. tour marking the organization’s centenary, Bhagwat said, “I heard some people say intense hatred is the basis of our work. It is just the reverse. ‘Shuddha Satvik Prem’ (pure and divine love) is the basis of our work.” 
Before landing in London, he had visited New York and Toronto. In New York, while addressing  a “Universal Oneness Celebration” at Madison Square Garden on August 29, Bhagwat said, “To call oneself Hindu, one must believe that all paths lead to the same destination and that every human has dignity, with no difference between human beings.” He described diversity as a “decoration for our innate unity” that has to be accepted: “It has to be respected. It has to be protected.”
In West Bengal, the next day, activists belonging to different RSS-linked organizations disrupted three separate Christian prayer gatherings and abused and heckled the prayer participants.
Here are some of the incidents, in just one Indian state, that took place during the same weeks Bhagwat was spreading the message of love and oneness abroad: 
August 23: A mob broke into a church premises at Uluberia in Howrah district, vandalized the prayer room, and attacked several prayer attendees. Bajrang Dal activists went to close down a Christian house prayer ceremony at Baniberia area in Mograhat of South 24 Parganas district. 
August 30: Bajrang Dal activists thrashed a lawyer for hosting Christian prayers at his residence in Baripur, South 24-Parganas. Miscreants stormed the Sunday prayer gathering at Jagatballabhpur, Howrah district. Another prayer venue was vandalized at Hingalganj in North 24 Parganas.  
September 1: Hindu Jagran Manch, another RSS affiliate, locked up a school run by Christians at Hasnabad Rupomari bazar in North 24 Parganas district. Protesters told the media: “Their walls are full of Jesus’ photos! No Hindu deities at all! Why should it be so? Why are they teaching kids about Jesus’ life? This school must be closed down.”
September 7: A group of activists claiming to be from the VHP and BD interrupted a prayer gathering at a tiny, makeshift church in Bally of Howrah district and told them that preaching Christianity will not be allowed. 
September 9: People identifying themselves as VHP and BD organizers reached a house at Mograhat area in South 24-Parganas district, aggressively quizzed people about who they worship, and objected to praying before Jesus. 
September 11: Bajrang Dal activists threatened the organizers of another prayer gathering at Mamudpur in Mograhat, South 24 Parganas. 
September 12: VHP activists threatened members of a house prayer gathering at Taldi, Canning, South 24 Parganas, ordered them to tear all of Jesus’ photos apart and sternly told them to stop the gathering for good. “Why Jesus? Why Jesus? Why Jesus?” they kept shouting. “Whoever you may be going to complain to, tell them that we are from VHP and Bajrang Dal. We’ll see who holds how much power.”  
The next day, another video went viral on social media that showed a Hindu supremacist mob violently abusing prayer gatherers and publicly tearing apart books on Param-pita (God the Father). “What the hell is ‘God the Father’? Why don’t you read the Gita or chant Hare Krishna?” the attackers shouted as they tore apart books on Christian faith.
articles.summary: From church vandalism to grave desecration, assaults against Christian minorities are increasing in the large state of West Bengal since the BJP, an RSS offshoot, came to power in May.

articles.title: From Symbolism to Strategy: The Expanding Operational Role of Women in Baloch Militancy
articles.full_text:
The motivations of individual women who join militant organizations cannot be reduced to a single explanation. The organizational incentives are easier to identify.
On May 22, the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA), one of the principal armed groups in Pakistan’s Baloch insurgency, announced the formation of a dedicated women’s wing and named Shaynaz Baloch as its commander. The announcement was significant not simply because it placed a woman in a more visible position within the organization, but because it appeared to formalize a trend that has been developing since 2022: the expansion of women’s participation in Baloch militancy from largely symbolic and support roles into direct operational activity.
The development raises a broader question: Why are Baloch militant organizations expanding women’s roles now, and what does this mean for an insurgency historically dominated by men?
The shift can be traced most clearly to April 2022, when Shari Baloch carried out a suicide attack at the Confucius Institute at the University of Karachi, killing three Chinese teachers and their Pakistani driver. The BLA claimed responsibility and presented her as its first female suicide operative. Since then, several other women have been linked to suicide operations attributed to BLA factions. In June 2023, Sumaiya Qalandrani Baloch carried out a suicide attack targeting a military convoy in Turbat. In August 2024, a woman identified by the BLA as Mahal Baloch conducted a vehicle-borne attack against a Frontier Corps facility in Bela. In March 2025, Mahikhan Baloch carried out another suicide attack against a paramilitary convoy in Kalat.  
In November 2025, the trend extended to another major Baloch armed group, the Baloch Liberation Front (BLF), when Zareena Rafiq carried out a vehicle-borne attack against a Frontier Corps facility in Nokundi. The pattern suggests that the use of women is no longer confined to an isolated form of militant propaganda. It is becoming part of how some Baloch armed groups recruit, operate, and present themselves. 
The development became even more visible during the BLA’s January-February 2026 offensive, which the organization called Operation Herof 2.0. The BLA publicized the participation of several women in the coordinated attacks, including female suicide operatives.
Balochistan, Pakistan’s largest province by area and one of its least densely populated, has experienced successive waves of Baloch nationalist insurgency, with the current conflict emerging in the early 2000s. The BLA and BLF are among the principal separatist organizations involved. They frame their campaigns around grievances including political marginalization, resource distribution, and alleged abuses by the Pakistani state. Pakistani authorities classify the groups as terrorist organizations and have attributed aspects of the insurgency to external support. The conflict has also acquired a significant international dimension. Balochistan hosts Gwadar Port and other major infrastructure associated with the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), making Chinese nationals and projects recurring targets for Baloch militants.
For much of the current insurgency, however, women associated with Baloch nationalism were more visible in political activism, advocacy, and community mobilization than in armed operations. Organizations such as the Baloch Students Organization-Azad (BSO-A) and the Baloch Yakjehti Committee have provided platforms for campaigns concerning enforced disappearances, alleged extrajudicial killings, and other grievances involving the Pakistani state. Women such as Mahrang Baloch and Sammi Deen Baloch have subsequently become prominent advocates on these issues. Karima Mehrab Baloch, who became the first woman to chair BSO-A, was another prominent figure in Baloch nationalist activism before she died in Toronto in December 2020.
This established a largely political role for women within the broader Baloch nationalist movement. But the emergence of women in militant operations since 2022 marks a departure from that pattern. The May announcement of a dedicated women’s wing in the BLA represents a potential further step in this evolution, from individual female participation in militant operations toward a more formal organizational role. 
The motivations of individual women who join militant organizations cannot be reduced to a single explanation. Political grievances, personal experiences, family or social networks, ideological commitment, trauma, and the search for purpose can all influence recruitment. These factors differ from one individual to another.
The organizational incentives are easier to identify. Women can provide militant groups with additional operational flexibility. Gendered assumptions about who constitutes a security threat can affect how individuals are screened, monitored, or approached by security personnel. This does not make women inherently better operatives. Rather, it gives organizations another category of personnel through which they can attempt to exploit gaps in security practices. Female participation can also broaden the pool from which militant organizations recruit. It allows groups to portray their struggle as extending beyond young male fighters and into families and communities.
The propaganda value may be even more important. A female militant challenges the conventional image of an insurgent as a young man carrying a weapon. Baloch militant groups have used photographs, videos, and biographies of female operatives to portray their participation as evidence that the conflict has reached across gender and social boundaries.
However, reducing female militants to passive victims of manipulation obscures their agency and the possibility that some make deliberate ideological or political choices. At the same time, focusing exclusively on agency can obscure the organizational structures that recruit, train, indoctrinate, and deploy them. The analytical challenge is to account for both. 
The Baloch case is part of a much broader history of women’s participation in political violence. Research on female suicide bombers has documented substantial participation by women in conflicts ranging from the Middle East to South Asia and Southeast Asia. Secular separatist organizations such as the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) and the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) were among the groups that developed significant roles for women in their military structures. The LTTE incorporated women into combat units and became particularly associated with female suicide operations. The PKK likewise developed extensive female military and organizational structures. 
Later, jihadist organizations including Boko Haram, al-Shabaab, and the Islamic State expanded women’s roles in different ways, including recruitment, propaganda, logistics, and, in some cases, direct participation in attacks. The comparison should not be overstated, however. These organizations differ substantially in ideology, structure, social environment, and strategic objectives. Baloch armed groups are primarily ethno-nationalist and separatist organizations rather than transnational jihadist movements. 
The expansion of women’s participation comes amid a broader deterioration in Pakistan’s security environment. The Baloch insurgency is only one component of that deterioration; the resurgence of the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), particularly along the Afghan border, has also contributed substantially to the country’s terrorism burden.
The Global Terrorism Index 2026 ranked Pakistan as the country most affected by terrorism in 2025, recording 1,139 terrorism-related deaths and 1,045 incidents. Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa together accounted for more than 74 percent of terrorist attacks and 67 percent of terrorism-related deaths recorded in Pakistan that year. This wider context matters because the emergence of female militants could tempt security institutions toward an overly broad response.
The answer is not simply increased surveillance of women. A poorly designed response could stigmatize women participating in legitimate political activity and further blur the distinction between peaceful activism and militancy. Instead, intelligence assessments should account for women as potential participants across the spectrum of militant activity, including recruitment, propaganda, financing, logistics, and direct operations. At the same time, investigators must distinguish genuine indicators of militant involvement from political dissent, human rights activism, and ordinary civic activity.
That distinction is particularly important in Balochistan, where a significant political and human rights movement exists alongside an armed insurgency. Conflating the two would not only threaten civil liberties; it could also make counterterrorism less effective by expanding the pool of people who feel alienated from the state. The strategic challenge is therefore twofold: prevent militant organizations from turning women’s visibility into an operational advantage, while ensuring that the state’s response does not itself deepen the alienation that those organizations seek to capitalize on. That means combining intelligence-led counterterrorism with community engagement, strategic communication, and efforts to address the grievances that militant organizations seek to exploit.

articles.title: Shipki La and the Battle Over the History of China-India Trade
articles.full_text:
The Chinese narrative attempts to erase the independent agency Tibet exercised before 1951, framing Shipki La as a historical link between China and India (not Tibet and India).
An illustration depicting the Shipki Pass, drawn in 1856.
After a six-year hiatus, the China-India border trade via Shipki Pass, a 3,930-meter pass in Himachal Pradesh’s Kinnaur district, resumed on August 1, 2026. After the 2020 Galwan military standoff, the border trade from this pass, often called the “Gateway to Tibet,” was suspended. With limited operations and economic scope but significant political symbolism, the resumption of border trade has also rejuvenated interest in the competing legitimacy narratives over the Tibet question. 
According to China’s state-affiliated think tanks and media, border trade via the Shipki L Pass dates to the 7th to 9th centuries when the Tubo Empire reigned over the plateau. China frames trade along this route as a sub-set of the Silk Road. Between the 14th and early 20th centuries, Chinese tellings claim Tibet as a commercial bridge between China and South Asia, while in the late 18th century, the Qing Dynasty of China took measures to standardize trade activities between Tibet and its neighboring countries, for “better management” of Tibet. 
As per the Chinese accounts, the “peaceful liberation” of Tibet in 1951 and the signing of the Panchsheel Pact led to the abolishment of India’s trade  “privileges” in Tibet and the formalization of a new paradigm for Indo-Tibetan trade. 
China claims to have set Sino-Indian border trade free from unequal terms set by colonial rule, ushering in an era of normalized development. Cut to the present: the reopening of Shipki La Pass, despite the minuscule trade volume, is received by Chinese media as a welcome move toward improving China-India strategic ties. 
Every aspect of the Chinese reading of history sidelines the Tibetan side of the story. For starters, what the Chinese narrative misses is the independent agency Tibet exercised before 1951. 
By contrast, Tibetan scholars characterize Shipki Pass as a major route for trade and cultural exchange between Indian territories and Tibet, independent of Chinese involvement. Consistent with Tibet’s claim to political and commercial autonomy, historical records describe Shipki Pass as a crucial route connecting Tibet with the Kingdom of Bushahar, Ladakh, and Kashmir. The exchange across the regions, involving a variety of products, was governed by gamgya, a traditional informal oath of mutual trust that was respected and maintained across generations. 
However, with the development of modern state infrastructure on either side of Shipki Pass and growing geopolitical disputes culminating in the Sino-Indian War in 1962, the centuries-old trade system was fractured. 
The Tibetan accounts also challenge the Chinese manipulation of history to appropriate the Shipki Pass trade route into a meta-narrative of the Silk Road. The commentaries consistent with the Tibetan narrative challenge the engulfing of Tibet in Chinese historical narratives as a simple commercial bridge, stripping it of its agency and independent existence. 
Tibetan scholars argue that it was the PRC’s administrative and military consolidation post 1951 that led to the dismantling of traditional trade and transit networks, not the British colonial disruption. The PRC’s normalization with India involved the isolation of Tibet and the enforcement of new restrictions on previously autonomous trade practices between India and Tibet
This is not a dispute over mere historical fact-checking. It leads to the question of who holds legitimacy over Tibet, and the framing of the India-China-Tibet relationship since the 1950s. 
The re-opening of Shipki Pass – often framed in terms of the overall China-India relationship – is seeing one version of history eclipse the other. Popular media crowds out the complicated, contesting narratives and historical claims by constructing a more attractive narrative around boosting local trade, development, and restoration of ancient ties. Given the meager economic value of this barter-driven border trade, the Chinese media has woven the narrative around regional livelihood, the possibility of infrastructure development, and building mutual trust. The Chinese commentary construes the opening as a “revival” of ancient Sino-Indian border trade, with Tibet as a commercial bridge, and part of efforts to eliminate the colonial inequalities after the “liberation of Tibet.” 
Over the last few years, the construction of border village resettlement projects, combining civilian housing with military and surveillance infrastructure, in the Tibet Autonomous Region near the Shipki Pass has gained momentum. These villages help give physical form to China’s version of the story, elevating ancient Sino-Indian trade ties over India-Tibet exchanges. Expanding beyond academic and journalistic narratives, Beijing is consolidating its rendition of Tibet as a commercial bridge through trade resumption and border infrastructure.
The reopening of Shipki Pass matters for reasons beyond trade resumption and China-India diplomacy. It highlights the disputes over sovereignty, history, and measures to consolidate control over the border. As it turns out, the trade diplomacy along the Sino-Indian border is less about trade and more about whose history triumphs.

articles.title: Infrastructure Gaps Test Pakistan’s Flagship CPEC Industrial Zone, Field Survey Finds
articles.full_text:
Even as investment tops 327 billion rupees, firms at Allama Iqbal Industrial City report inadequate wastewater infrastructure, unreliable utilities, and no public transport.
Allama Iqbal Industrial City in Faisalabad, Pakistan.
FAISALABAD — Allama Iqbal Industrial City (AIIC), the first Special Economic Zone prioritized under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), has drawn more than 327 billion rupees ($1.2 billion) in committed investment and allotted 223 of 424 planned plots. But a field survey of the zone’s authority and four operating firms – including a China-Pakistan joint venture – found that basic infrastructure has not kept pace with that investment. The zone management itself now lists the resulting gaps among its most urgent priorities.
The survey was conducted on-site using structured research instruments and covered Faisalabad Industrial Estate Development & Management Company (FIEDMC), which administers the 3,966-acre zone along the M-4 Motorway, and four operating firms; the findings are diagnostic rather than statistically representative. It found that water is supplied only through self-boring – individual firms drilling and managing their own wells – because no zone-wide piped potable network exists. Sewerage infrastructure remains under construction, while the zone’s assessment indicates that no Combined Effluent Treatment Plant (CETP) has yet been funded, leaving firms to manage industrial wastewater largely on their own.
“CETP and utility reliability” was the single most urgent reform named by FIEDMC’s own senior officials – spanning its general manager for engineering and its estate, zone, and land managers – when asked directly what the AIIC needs most. They also flagged the need to make the zone’s “One-Window Operation” facilitation service fully functional and time-bound, and to establish dedicated public transport and stronger security for workers commuting to the site.
Those official priorities broadly align with concerns reported by the four tenant firms surveyed independently. Ocean Ceramics, a wall-tile manufacturer employing 230 people at the AIIC since 2022, said in its response that “transport facilities are not available for local travelling” and that mobile signal and internet coverage across the zone is weak and slow – potentially constraining firms that increasingly depend on digital systems for customs filling and coordination with overseas buyers. The firm reported annual revenue of 1-5 billion rupees, but currently exports none of its output. Ocean Ceramics said reduced gas and electricity costs would do more than anything else to improve its performance.
A China-Pakistan steel joint venture that entered the zone in 2024 with 88 employees reported similar concerns about shared infrastructure, rating the zone’s common effluent-treatment and testing facilities only average. 
Among the zone officials surveyed, customs facilitation ranked as the most serious barrier to exports at the AIIC – ahead even of energy costs, which firms described as “costly” rather than simply scarce. The survey found that AIIC currently has no on-site warehousing, logistics, or customs facilities of any kind – all three were explicitly marked “not included” in the zone’s own infrastructure assessment. 
For a zone being developed as an export-oriented manufacturing hub under CPEC, the absence of such basic trade infrastructure is a striking finding, and one that officials say compounds the customs delay already facing exporters.
Equally notable is what the four-firm sample reveals about how some firms operate once inside the SEZ. Of the four companies surveyed, three – including the China-Pakistan venture – reported no supply or sourcing relationships with any other AIIC tenant, describing themselves as operating as stand-alone units rather than as part of an integrated industrial cluster. Only Matco Foods, a food-processing exporter with 250 employees, reported a working intra-zone linkage, sourcing construction steel from a neighboring tenant. 
Two of the four firms surveyed, including the China-Pakistan steel venture, reported exporting none of their output at all. FIEDMC’s own records on firm-level export performance – the number of exporting firms, export value, and destination markets – were left entirely blank, suggesting that systematic firm-level tracking of exports remains incomplete.
Since its 2020 notification, the zone has attracted 117 investors, drawing 147 billion rupees in foreign capital and 180.53 billion rupees in domestic investment – figures consistent with the more than $1 billion in commitments publicly reported by Pakistan’s Board of Investment. Investors from China, Germany, Switzerland, Canada, and the Netherlands sit alongside a large base of domestic firms.
Field work adds a granularity often missing from official announcements. The picture, drawn directly from the zone’s operators and tenants, is that of a flagship CPEC project whose investment pipeline has outpaced the utilities, logistics, and transport infrastructure needed to convert that investment into functioning, export-ready industry. 
With FIEDMC’s own leadership now naming utility reliability, streamlined customs facilitation, and worker transport as top priorities, the findings point less to a dispute between government and industry than to a shared, and increasingly urgent, agenda for the next phase of the AIIC’s development.
The next measure of the AIIC’s success, therefore, should not be how many plots are allotted or how much investment is committed, but how effectively those investments are converted into operating factories, industrial linkages, exports, and jobs.

articles.title: The Nexperia Case Was Actually a Success. Does Europe Know That?
articles.full_text:
A combination of media misunderstandings, Chinese distortions, and Dutch mistakes raise the risk that Europeans draw the wrong conclusions about economic security.
The July 2026 meeting between Dutch Trade Minister Sjoerd Sjoerdsma and China’s Commerce Minister Wang Wentao was cordial. That might have come as a surprise given the tensions that erupted between China and the Netherlands following a high-profile dispute about Nexperia in the fall of 2025. The new Dutch government made it clear that it wanted to patch up ties with Beijing.
Underneath the mess, the Nexperia incident was actually a comparatively successful economic security intervention – and that carries important lessons for Europe.
At the July 2026 talks, the Chinese side called on the Dutch to “promote the proper resolution of disputes involving relevant companies,” a clear reference to the Nexperia case. Meanwhile The Hague is keen to let the courts move ahead. 
Nexperia’s Chinese owner, Wingtech, claims Nexperia China is now an independent producer, while Nexperia expects the worst shortages on the European side to ease by year’s end. China’s position of power means that a split of the company appears unavoidable, but at least its European business was saved.
There remain many uncertain factors, not the least Wingtech’s arbitration procedure against the Dutch state incorrectly claiming expropriation while a court case that could permanently replace management is underway. Yet, a combination of not all Anglophone press fully grasping what really happened, Chinese distortion of the facts, and some Dutch ministerial amateurism raise the risk that Europeans draw the wrong conclusions about a vital policy area.
Acting on the back-foot in response to a clear threat to European economic security, the Dutch economic affairs minister and Nexperia’s European leadership faced Beijing’s usual recipe of escalating to force the other to de-escalate when they moved to protect the automotive chip manufacturer. The minister’s moves should have been planned better, yet it was necessary to finally call a halt to the company’s hollowing out by its Chinese owners. If European countries want to avoid high long-term costs, they not only need to face the disproportionate short-term costs that Beijing will seek to inflict but also accept that any wins will only ever be partial.
The story of Nexperia is one of several interventions that lacked sufficient force to change the overall trajectory. Things only came to a head when the remaining choice was between biting the bullet and losing everything. The company’s importance to supply chains was not fully appreciated when it was created out of the low-margin Standard Products unit of NXP Semiconductors – itself carved out of Philips in 2006.
In 2017, this new Nexperia was sold to Chinese state-backed funds JAC Capital and Wise Road. The next year, the two funds organized a closed-door auction of the company only open to Chinese bidders. The winner was Wingtech, a small company with no serious experience in the field. These sales were little remarked on in the years before the EU enacted its FDI screening. At the time, Chinese investment was welcome. In fact, two other Philips Semiconductor components also moved to Chinese ownership: chip designer Goodix and Ampleon.
Despite promises to prevent leakage at the time of takeover, former CEO Frans Scheper told Dutch television that it was clear Wingtech’s Zhang Xuezheng tried to turn Nexperia into a Chinese company from the beginning. Nexperia’s European directors were largely unaware of Zhang’s checkered record in China, where he had been sentenced to prison in 2005 for unlawfully obtaining ZTE trade secrets and fined in 2024 for concealing shareholdings back in 2017. The Dutch civilian intelligence agency AIVD was asking questions about Zhang in 2019, but nothing came of it.
The first sign of external trouble stemming from Chinese ownership came a few years later. In November 2022, the U.K. government forced Nexperia to reverse the acquisition of a fab in Newport. The company started talks with the Dutch Economic Affairs Ministry about governance reforms that would allow it to be treated like a European company, after it missed out on German chip funds in 2023. Nexperia’s customers pressured it to address concerns and diversify. 
When Wingtech was put on the Entity List by the U.S. government in December 2024, engagement with the ministry intensified. Rather than solving the problems, those typically Dutch talks ended up triggering the Chinese management.
As time wore on, the Europeans began to believe that Zhang was acting in bad faith in multiple ways. In China, he had been setting up parallel structures with his WingSkySemi (WSS) fab in Shanghai under his own Wentianxia holding. The Chinese owners stopped the incomplete expansion of its Malaysian assembly center, despite customer demand. Zhang was focused on China, where his true interests lie. 
When the talks between Nexperia and the Dutch government honed in on governance changes, the Chinese owners began to fear they would lose control. A Chinese legal firm was brought in to advise. Matters came to a head when Wingtech allegedly violated Dutch company law to remove European directors and give unqualified Chinese officers financial control.
This is when the interventions happened. Both the Dutch ministry and Nexperia’s European managers told the court there were imminent plans to move R&D and production to China. Zhang supposedly drew up a plan using DeepSeek and ChatGPT that would have entailed laying off almost half the European staff. The court filings accuse Zhang of placing an unnecessarily large order of $200 million from his own WSS fab in Shanghai. Talks were no longer enough to resolve this chasm in understanding.
Now the dust has settled, all that remains of the interventions is the Dutch court order. All attention has been drawn to Dutch and U.S. government actions; however, the real effects stemmed from the specific nature of the Dutch system. That legal route is precisely why The Hague cannot be forced by Beijing to reverse what has happened.
The world learned about the Enterprise Chamber of the Amsterdam Court of Appeals – the court responsible for corporate matters – in October 2024. Nexperia’s chief legal officer had turned to the court accusing Zhang of mismanagement, joined by the workers’ council. 
The Dutch Ministry of Economic Affairs had been aware beforehand and moved first. Afraid that Zhang would act to forestall the case by firing the directors, Vincent Karremans – then the minister of economic affairs – issued an unprecedented instruction under never-used Cold War legislation to put the company under special supervision. The next day, on October 1, the Amsterdam court issued its first of several provisional rulings that suspended the Chinese owners’ powers over a company that remained in their possession.
The timing was unfortunate, coming just as Washington announced a rule that would have extended Wingtech’s Entity List status to its subsidiary, Nexperia. Allegedly, The Hague had even lobbied Washington to postpone the announcement to prevent the resulting conflation of U.S. action, Dutch ministerial instruction, and the Nexperia directors’ litigation. 
In hindsight, the Dutch minister’s politically sensitive instruction was perhaps never necessary and is now suspended. The U.S. export controls were suspended for a year on November 10, 2025 as part of the Trump–Xi truce. What has actually impacted Nexperia is the Dutch legal system and its unique conception of corporate governance.
The first notion that allowed the court to play its role was Nexperia’s European directors’ accusations against the Chinese owners of “wanbestuur”’ – mismanagement, harming the interests of the legal entity they were responsible for in pursuit of personal gain. This concept may be harder to understand for businesspeople from China or Silicon Valley, given their obsession with the intrepid founder juggling various legal entities and jurisdictions to create an empire. However, in the Netherlands the swashbuckling Zhang ran into a rather different view. Dutch enterprise law protects firms against directors – even if the owners originally brought the entity into being in order to exploit it.
A second component that outside observers missed in the Nexperia case is the Netherlands’ so-called polder model, related to “tripartism” in English. The idea is that the government, employers, and workers come together to discuss and agree on the issues in a game of give-and-take. The Netherlands’ traditionally relatively autonomous ministries often seem to represent their respective fields within the government based on the consensuses they have reached with their stakeholders. The condition, however, for a ministry to go to bat for you is engaging in good faith in tripartite engagements. A Chinese company should be able to comprehend that notion of cooperating with the government.
The talks between the Economic Affairs Ministry and Nexperia on governance reforms were held under those conditions. Wingtech’s failure to renew Nexperia’s collective bargaining agreement with the trade unions demonstrated its misunderstanding of the “voluntary” nature of such talks. The reporting suggested a genuine desire by a perhaps somewhat naïve Dutch ministry to help find a way to have the company treated as European. Zhang appears to have never cared about the European nuances.
It seems likely that the Dutch Economic Affairs Ministry expected a similar outcome to an earlier case. Just the year before, in 2024, the ministry had supported the CEO of Ampleon – another former subsidiary of Philips Semiconductor bought by a Chinese owner – when he also turned to the same Enterprise Chamber in secret. The problem was similar: a Chinese owner planning to move research capacity to Shanghai. The result was a settlement in 2025 with continued Chinese ownership under safeguards against IP-leakage. That case remained secret until the newspaper FD revealed that it had happened at all in April 2026. 
Beyond the minister’s instruction and lack of U.S. factor, something else was different in Nexperia’s case: Zhang Xuezheng.
China’s Decentralized Industrial Coercion
The threat of hollowing out that Nexperia faced was the consequence of China’s decentralized industrial policy, but the coercion that followed the economic security intervention was centrally directed. While many abroad did not understand the nature of the Dutch system, The Hague’s actions showed key actors likewise did not fully appreciate this aspect of the Chinese system.
In China, swashbuckling founders like Zhang Xuezheng are not uncommon – in fact, entrepreneurial businesspeople like him are actively enabled by the state. The Chinese party-state creates a centrally-determined industrial policy that is executed locally, something often misunderstood by Europeans. Beijing sets incentives that motivate not just people like Zhang but also their local home governments to pursue central goals. Certain key strategic sectors, such as the quest to replace ASML, are centrally led, but most – including not only electric vehicles but also the less flashy parts of the semiconductor industry – are the result of local public-private entrepreneurship.
Reading the Dutch press and court documents, it seems that Nexperia was used as a tool for Zhang’s grand plans for a tech empire inside China. His personal benefit coincided with incentives that spurred local government to act in support of China’s quest for industrial dominance – such as helping build Zhang’s independent WSS fab. The neglect of Nexperia’s business outside of China was the result of systematic indifference that this focus engendered. Yet for Beijing these effects are by design, even when specific cases like this one are not planned.
The Dutch Economic Affairs Ministry’s unsophisticated approach subsequently turned this locally-supported process into a political challenge that elevated the issue to the central level. The minister’s intervention and the court’s ruling were conflated due to The Hague’s lack of communication, China’s limited understanding of the Dutch system, and Beijing’s deliberate distortion. However, once the Dutch action on Nexperia had become a public challenge to China, Beijing had no choice but to publicly intervene anyway.
articles.summary: A combination of media misunderstandings, Chinese distortions, and Dutch mistakes raise the risk that Europeans draw the wrong conclusions about economic security.

articles.title: Making the Most Out of Growing US-Uzbekistan Trade and Investment
articles.full_text:
Uzbekistan aims to attract greater U.S. investment, and is making its own investments in the United States. But it can’t forget the people.
Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev (center) with Sergio Gor (right), special envoy for South and Central Asia, and U.S. Senator Steve Daines (left), co-chair of the Senate Central Asia Caucus.
The purchase of U.S.-made commercial aircraft and an Uzbek company’s historic opening of a manufacturing facility in Kentucky demonstrate the dynamic and growing economic relations between the United States and Uzbekistan. As U.S. diplomatic engagement with Tashkent increases – new contracts and trade and investment frameworks signed – understanding each country’s priorities and objectives will help explain this new chapter of the partnership. Moreover, stronger trade and investment numbers must translate into employment opportunities and an improved quality of life for the Uzbek population.
Relations between Washington and Tashkent have generally strengthened over the past couple of years. U.S. President Donald Trump and Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev will next meet in December, as Trump has invited the Uzbek leader to be a guest at the G-20 summit in Miami.
Stronger diplomatic links are translating into trade and investment deals. In June, the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) Ambassador Jamieson Greer visited Tashkent and signed “an early harvest of trade commitments to strengthen the bilateral economic and investment relationship.” Specifically, Tashkent committed “to eliminate or reduce tariffs” on U.S. industrial goods and agricultural products. In contrast, Washington committed “to provide favorable consideration” in tariff actions for Uzbekistan’s industrial goods and agricultural products. The two sides are also working to conclude an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade and Investment.
Also in June, the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) launched the U.S.-Uzbekistan Joint Investment Platform, which will “aim to identify strategic investments in Uzbekistan for U.S.” in areas like energy, infrastructure, critical minerals, transportation and logistics infrastructure.
The topic of investment in critical minerals, energy, and transportation was also reportedly discussed during a meeting between Mirziyoyev and Sergio Gor, the U.S. special envoy for South and Central Asian affairs, on the sidelines of the recent Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan.
This activity builds upon the momentum of earlier deals. In 2025, Tashkent announced a $8.5 billion deal to buy as many as 22 Boeing 787 Dreamliner aircraft to modernize the country’s commercial aviation industry. The aircraft will allow direct, long-distance flights with the United States, increasing connectivity and tourism.
Investment now goes both ways, breaking stereotypes and assumptions of the U.S. being the only actor in the Central Asia-U.S. relationships that invests on the other side. The Uzbek company AFKA is building a manufacturing facility in Bowling Green, Kentucky. It will be the first Uzbek manufacturing company to operate in the U.S. The groundbreaking ceremony took place in July, and when complete, the AFKA Aluminum Solutions plant will employ 331 people, supporting the local economy and strengthening bilateral commercial ties.
Stronger economic links between the two governments occur at a time when Tashkent is looking to develop the entire country, not just the capital. For example, the historic city of Khiva is getting a face-lift through the expected construction of a conference hall, a 3-star hotel, and a reception house, which will create jobs and attract tourism. Plans also include building a toll road and a railway to connect the Urgench airport with Khiva. Other plans include modernizing regional airports to improve domestic and international connectivity.
As for Nukus, the capital of the Republic of Karakalpakstan, the goal is to upgrade the city’s public transportation via a loan from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.
From Washington’s perspective, there is a new race on to access resources like oil, gas, and especially critical minerals. Central Asia has been blessed with many of the resources that the world’s great powers desire. Central Asian governments like Uzbekistan view this situation not as a game or a race but as an opportunity to build new commercial partnerships and attract investors. While the Trump administration continues to focus on energy, minerals, and transportation infrastructure as vital areas for future investment and trade, Tashkent can hopefully also redirect U.S. interest to other projects and industries.
For example, during the November 2025 summit between Trump and the five Central Asian leaders, Washington pledged to explore “the expansion of a partnership in the upcoming sale and privatization of UzAuto Motors” in addition to a potential $3 billion investment from Air Products for a methanol production facility in Uzbekistan. The Uzbek government aims to generate 54 percent of its power from renewable sources by 2030. Washington and Tashkent hope to encourage U.S. companies to invest in this field.
There are limitations to consider, specifically the Jackson-Vanik Amendment, which denies permanent normal trade relations to Uzbekistan. To be fair, while the amendment irritates political relations, its impact on bilateral trade and investment is negligible. Tashkent has, for decades, received temporary normal trade relations through annual presidential waivers.
Moreover, even if U.S.-Uzbek trade grows considerably, it will still be dwarfed by trade between Uzbekistan and China, which reached between $7.7 and $8.9 billion in the first half of the year. Simply put, stronger U.S.-Uzbek trade and investment ties will not dramatically create a new architecture of priority partners for Uzbekistan.
There is also a domestic component to consider: Uzbekistan has the region’s largest population, with around 39 million (according to a new census), and a vast young workforce who deserve jobs and a future in their homeland. Unfortunately, a significant portion of the population lives below the poverty line, and unemployment is still problematic, more than a million Uzbeks migrate abroad for work every year.
As in many countries, wealth and development concentrate in the capital. While the examples of regional infrastructure development mentioned in this commentary are positive, a 2025 study conducted by the National Statistics Committee of Uzbekistan in collaboration with the World Bank showed that the largest numbers of poor residents were recorded in the Samarkand region (265,000 people), as well as in Fergana (239,000), Kashkadarya (238,000), and Andijan (214,000) regions.
In other words, Uzbekistan must invest more in infrastructure projects and economic growth across its regions, not just the capital.
In a September 3 speech, Mirziyoyev said a new system to reduce poverty and unemployment across the country will be introduced. This new strategy must be monitored to ensure it promotes employment and helps low-income individuals, rather than falling victim to bureaucratic incompetence or corruption.
As interest in Central Asia’s natural resources continues to grow, it is also important to understand the priorities of the five Central Asian governments. In Uzbekistan, the momentum is to diversify the country’s energy production and bring development to areas outside Tashkent. Washington and American industries must keep Tashkent’s priorities and objectives in mind to secure win-win contracts and agreements and ensure this partnership continues as the so-called race for critical minerals heats up.
For Uzbekistan’s population, particularly those living outside Tashkent, this stronger partnership must mean more jobs, economic growth, and a better quality of life.
The purchase of U.S.-made commercial aircraft and an Uzbek company’s historic opening of a manufacturing facility in Kentucky demonstrate the dynamic and growing economic relations between the United States and Uzbekistan. As U.S. diplomatic engagement with Tashkent increases – new contracts and trade and investment frameworks signed – understanding each country’s priorities and objectives will help explain this new chapter of the partnership. Moreover, stronger trade and investment numbers must translate into employment opportunities and an improved quality of life for the Uzbek population.
Relations between Washington and Tashkent have generally strengthened over the past couple of years. U.S. President Donald Trump and Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev will next meet in December, as Trump has invited the Uzbek leader to be a guest at the G-20 summit in Miami.

The aircraft will allow direct, long-distance flights with the United States, increasing connectivity and tourism.

articles.title: 4 Fault Lines that Could Shape the Trump-Xi Summit
articles.full_text:
The tangible outcomes will be modest, but the stakes are high.
U.S. President Donald Trump participates in a welcome ceremony with China’s President Xi Jinping at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, China, May 14, 2026.
U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are set to meet next week at the White House in Washington, D.C., provided that the “conditionalities” attached to the summit are met. This will be the second leaders’ summit between Trump and Xi this year, following the U.S. president’s visit to Beijing in May. 
This will be Xi’s first visit to the U.S. capital in a decade, after he met then-U.S. President Barack Obama in 2016. Back then, the agenda centered on the much-touted issues of cyberespionage and commercial hacking. Today, there are new concerns. 
Both domestically and internationally, this visit is taking place amid considerable friction. On the domestic front, the United States will be holding midterm elections roughly 40 days after the visit. This makes the timing an unusual choice, as noted by Pew Research: many Americans still view the Chinese leader unfavorably, despite a 6-percentage-point rise since last year. Presidents generally avoid such risks to optics as midterms near. 
At the international level, the world is still living under the shadow of the Iran-U.S. war. Consequently, Brent crude is trading around $100 per barrel. At the same time, the China-Russia alignment has deepened; a few months ago – just after the last Trump-Xi summit, in fact – Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin reaffirmed their close partnership and signed a joint statement to deepen their strategic partnership. Beijing is underwriting Moscow’s war machine in Ukraine as Washington prepares to welcome Xi. 
Meanwhile, Pew Research noted in another survey that Beijing is viewed favorably in more countries than Washington, adding another nuance to the global attention focused on the summit.
However, one must note that Beijing has yet to officially confirm the meeting, even though the United States has given the date of September 24. Some reports even suggested that the meeting will be canceled by Beijing if Washington gives approval for a $14 billion arms sale to Taiwan. 
Therefore, the coming week will tell us much about the relationship between China and the United States.
Even assuming the meeting does go ahead as planned, there are low expectations for what will be achieved. The consensus holds that the tangible outcomes will be modest, possibly just an extension of what was achieved at the last summit held in China. There are four topics of particular interest at the Trump-Xi summit.
First is the tariff question. At the Trump-Xi meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Busan, South Korea, on October 30, 2025, Washington and Beijing agreed to a one-year truce in their trade war. The United States reduced its fentanyl-related tariff on Chinese goods to 10 percent. The U.S. also suspended a 10 percent reciprocal tariff and secured a commitment from Beijing to buy 25 million tons of U.S. soybeans every year through 2028. China also deferred export controls on rare earths. But this truce will expire in November this year. 
The upcoming Trump-Xi meeting will build on these arrangements rather than introduce something entirely novel. Already, the rare earth element in the deal is quite fragile. Some reports have suggested that exports of yttrium – a rare earth element used in the aerospace and defense industries – to the United States have declined sharply after April 2025, despite China’s commitment to waive export controls. Some U.S. officials and analysts have discussed imposing new tariffs and charges on certain Chinese goods. This could be used as leverage in negotiations before the meeting. 
The second focal point is Iran. The ceasefire in the Middle East has collapsed multiple times, a recurring feature of Trump’s foreign policy. Just over a week ago, Iran retaliated against the U.S. strikes on the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and hit Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait, and Iraq. 
China is currently Iran’s largest trading partner and the top buyer of its oil, and Washington has declared economic war on Iran. In practice, as Iran is already heavily sanctioned, the new U.S. Treasury Department campaign – dubbed “Operation Economic Outcast” – involves pressuring those who “enabled” Iran’s actions. 
Trump mentioned speaking directly to Xi over this and asking him not to get involved. In May, both China and the United States agreed that Iran should not have a nuclear weapon, but this small point of agreement is being overshadowed by the heightening tension over other issues. 
Third is Taiwan. Taiwan has long remained a thorn in China-U.S. relations. After the summit held in May 2026, Trump called U.S. arms sales to Taiwan a “very good negotiating chip” that he kept in abeyance. This transactional framing alarmed many of the U.S. allies. Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te immediately pushed back against it by declaring that the sovereignty of the island will not be “sacrificed or traded away.” 
More recently, reports emerged that China had threatened to cancel the summit if Trump approved the sale. Getting Washington to agree, even temporarily, to halt arms sales to Taiwan has been a major priority for Beijing since the 1980s. Now that Trump has signaled a willingness to view arms sales as a bargaining chip, rather than a routine aspect of the Taiwan-U.S. relationship, Xi will be looking to lock in that mindset. 
Even if the sale eventually gets approved, the fact that it is seen as a point of leverage by Trump shows the limits of his interest in Taiwan for its own sake. This problem extends well beyond Taiwan itself. Manila’s ongoing standoff with Beijing over maritime features in the South China Sea, notably Scarborough Shoal, is seen by allies as a test of whether Washington will prioritize optics with Beijing over its interests. If Trump signals that he will, not only Taiwan but Tokyo, Manila, and others can interpret their security guarantees as “negotiable,” especially when they clash with China. This will test the whole alliance architecture in Asia. 
The fourth area to watch is AI, which is at the heart of the U.S. strategy on China. Under the Biden administration, export controls effectively banned advanced AI chips from reaching China. Trump also tightened these restrictions in April 2025. However, he sharply reversed that policy between December 2025 and January 2026. The administration changed its approach to Nvidia’s H200 chips from a “presumption of denial” of exports to China to case-by-case approval. Chinese firms placed orders for millions of H200 chips. Trump touted it as a business deal, not as a national security issue. This caused some alarm and pushback within the United States.
On the other hand, even strict export control rules are easy to circumvent. Big Chinese firms like ByteDance, Alibaba, and Tencent have been using Nvidia chips sourced from third countries such as Japan, Thailand, and Malaysia rather than shipping them directly into China. 
Amid all these controls, China is still progressing well in AI, though it remains behind the United States. However, their models now account for a much larger share of global AI usage than before, thanks to China’s open-weight strategies and more efficient models. Such contradictions in the U.S. policy will be very visible in the upcoming meetings. 
Anyone hoping for a serious discussion on AI safety regulations, meanwhile, is likely to be disappointed. While there have been rumors of upcoming AI talks around the time of the Trump-Xi summit, both states see themselves locked in competition for dominance of AI, and are unlikely to pump the brakes. 
India will be closely watching all developments in Washington next week. Last year, Trump left no stone unturned in pressuring India, adding a 50 percent tariff on Indian goods in response to New Delhi’s continued purchases of Russian oil. Trump himself, after seeing Xi, Putin, and India’s Narendra Modi together in a summit last year, posted that the U.S. had “lost India and Russia to deepest, darkest, China.” In February 2026, a framework India-U.S. deal eased the effective tariff rate from 50 percent to 18 percent, but the damage to the trust was already done. 
Just days before the upcoming Trump-Xi meeting, Xi was in Delhi for the BRICS summit; both governments said they were committed to working toward the border dispute, resuming direct flights and relaxing investment restrictions. The New Delhi Declaration also voiced opposition to unilateral imposition of tariffs and trade restrictions and called for reform in the multipolar global order. However, genuine issues still prevail between New Delhi and Beijing. 
Seen from New Delhi, therefore, the meeting next week will signal to India where it stands in Washington’s priorities and whether Trump’s transactional policy continues to impact India-U.S. ties. Many countries will be watching the summit for similar signs, meaning the ripples will spread far beyond bilateral China-U.S. relations.

articles.title: Drones Offer Central Asia an Escape From Foreign Dependency
articles.full_text:
Central Asian states should jointly develop drone capabilities to prepare for current and future security needs.
Drones are everywhere in the news and on the frontlines of the Iran-U.S. War and the Russia-Ukraine War, but their most recent use on a battlefield in Central Asia represents a long-term issue – continued dependency on foreign suppliers. The Central Asian states may just be replacing their long-term Russian security dependency with a Turkish one.
Central Asian leaders risk deepening this dependency and worsening security vulnerabilities as they announce deals with foreign suppliers that are often headquartered in a single state – Turkiye. However, developments in 2026 show that opportunities for local development and production that would benefit regional economies without offloading security responsibilities exist. Local politicians just need to invest locally.
In the 2022 border conflict between Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, Turkiye’s Baykar Bayraktar TB2 unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) played a well-publicized role. After that conflict, Bishkek decided to deepen its Turkish dependency, ordering Aksungur and Akinci platforms, both from Turkish manufacturers, TAI and Baykar, respectively. It had already ordered additional TB2s and Anka (from TAI) as well.
Drones are certainly cheaper than manned aircraft, but these imported platforms weren’t without cost. Civil servants took a pay hit to fund the purchase of the new systems. And this doesn’t factor in the cost of operations and maintenance. To keep these aircraft flying with spare parts, ammunition, and sensors will require continual funding. When buying any big-ticket item, that platform is committing the state to long-term sustainment with certain suppliers.
Given Turkiye’s mercurial defense policy in recent years, can Bishkek rely on adequate sustainment in the event of another conflict? Turkiye, a NATO ally, hoped to procure F-35s, but acquired Russian S-400s, and is reportedly trying to resell those air defense system to the UAE, before aiming to rejoin F-35 talks. In addition to the initial procurement, depending on a foreign supplier means worrying about receiving additional parts and frames to replace losses from wear and tear or combat operations.  
Russia and Ukraine initially looked to foreign support for their attritive war. Tehran supplied Moscow with propeller-driven one-way attack Shahed-136 drones within the first year of the conflict. Yet, Moscow soon realized that the battlefield demanded the systems evolve. Manufacturing facilities were set up inside Russia and improvements were applied to the platform including jet power, anti-radar materials, and better guidance (the latest Russian-made version is dubbed the Geran-4/5).
A similar learning process happened on Kyiv’s side. Chinese-made DJI Mavics, Turkish TB2s, and American Switchblades provided early inventory for Ukrainian forces. Yet, soon manufacturing was moved in country and development processes brought closer to the frontlines, to incorporate the daily lessons of countermeasures, deception, and the realities of a non-permissive battlespace.
While the support systems needed to keep UAVs aloft are simpler than those required for fighters, the current Iran-U.S. War – a much more permissive environment than that in eastern Ukraine – has shown how vulnerable drones are to anti-air capabilities. The U.S. has lost 45 MQ-9 Reaper tactical UAVs, 25 percent of its fleet, since the start of the campaign. Given the years and cost to replace its vehicles, the Pentagon may just switch over to different systems altogether. 
Perhaps as a response to its competition and conflict with Bishkek, Dushanbe turned to its own foreign partner to develop a UAV capability. Around the same time, in 2022, it was reported that a program to produce, likely assemble, Iranian Ababil-2s in Tajikistan, was reached. At the signing were Iranian Major General Mohammad Bagheri and Tajik Defense Minister Sherali Mirzo. Bagheri was killed in Israeli air strikes in 2025 and Mirzo was shuffled out of office the same year. 
It is unclear how much progress has been made with this facility, or if this was all just a smoke screen. Yet, even if this project had gotten off the ground, it is hard to see how that would not have resulted in significant risk. Manufacturing drones for Tehran could very quickly bring banking and dollar restrictions from Washington, making such a venture a real security risk and potential big money-loser. Ultimately, this appears to be four years with only minimal progress on UAV capabilities for Tajikistan. 
Given the pitfalls of foreign dependency, Central Asia may look to develop its own systems, or at the very least license the full production process for its own domestically manufactured unmanned systems. First off, the costs are not prohibitive, unlike, say, developing an armored vehicle, ship, or manned aircraft. Second, the scale and security needs in the region are sufficient to support domestic UAV production.  
Third, regional states already have a start on the research, development, and manufacturing needed to make such cooperation a success. Finally, the opportunities of joint drone research and production could lead to increased security cooperation along borders and against transnational threats. Doing so will help to escape the pitfalls of learned incapacity. What’s key though is that local leaders invest in R&D domestically – not outsource solutions.
Take for example the Kyrgyz company Nanospace that announced in May 2026 plans to open a UAV institute in Tash-Dobo, just outside Bishkek. This plan is still in its infancy, but training operators and developing technologies to network numerous small drones is an important step in developing domestic air defense, research, and surveillance, capabilities that are not dependent on foreign assistance. 
Central Asia is already a regional education destination. This will continue, unless domestic actors eliminate academic freedom and quell basic research. Eurasian students have long come to Kyrgyzstan for higher education, whether at the University of Central Asia or the American University of Central Asia. Kazakhstan is a major international academic hub now as well, with some 30,000-plus foreign students attending branch institutions of Cardiff and Woosong, as well as attending homegrown universities like Al Farabi and Eurasian National. So, there are major opportunities to network skills and technologies that could benefit human capital and defense development for the entire region. 
Meanwhile, an exhibit in the late summer of 2026 in Uzbekistan highlighted a new Shunqor-8 drone interceptor from the Center for Innovative Technologies that could serve as a cheap alternative to traditional missile defense. Usually, Russian exports have provided most of the region’s air defense. In recent years, for example, even amid a war that is demanding major stocks of air defenses, Kyrgyzstan demonstrated S-300PS and Tor-M2KM (long- and short-range) SAMs and Tajikistan took deliveries from Russia.
The region still connects to legacy CIS Joint Air Defense System (ADS), so this is another important step in terms of Central Asia states providing for their own defense. Boilerplate statements suggested “modernizing” the ADS and advancing cooperation in 2026, though there was a mention of AI being integrated. In addition, the quantities being delivered to the region are likely insufficient for any prolonged conflict. Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan already have experience with joint venture manufacturing lines. There’s no reason for Central Asian states to continue to procure UAVs from abroad rather than building them (even with licenses) at home. 
Now, clearly the region won’t replace every imported component with a domestic analogue. Local manufacturers, for example, are unlikely to compete in the international market for electro-optical/infrared sensors. Yet, for smaller first-person view UAVs, and tactical UAVs, there’s plenty of room for choices in terms of cameras for reconnaissance or navigation systems that are mapped to the local environment and do not depend on one satellite network. Anticipating such payload flexibility can help Central Asian states avoid getting “locked in” to one new partner that just supplants the old one. 
One-way attack (OWA) drones are another opportunity for Central Asian states to better, more effectively, target security threats. One of the issues in recent combat operations has been an employment of seemingly indiscriminate or inaccurate artillery fire and combat aircraft strikes. OWA drones offer a way to address this and safeguard civilian lives. For example, during the 2022 Tajik-Kyrgyz conflict, indiscriminate artillery shelling and automatic weapons fire contributed to significant civilian casualties in Khistevarz, Ovchi Kalacha, Ak-Sai, and Margun, among other locations. 
In much earlier conflicts, manned aircraft with unguided weapons were ineffective, or suffered significant casualties, including in Rasht and the Ferghana Valley region. The cost of manned combat aircraft is such that most states in the region cannot afford such a fleet. And in any case, even if affordable, this still leads to foreign dependency. Training and education, parts and repairs, and operations even depended in large part on Russia. Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan are not unique in this, but surely this is an opportunity to reduce civilian casualties in conflict zones and limit reliance on a foreign power.
Finally, there are a host of interconnected challenges that drones can help the region address. Everything from detecting smuggling and trafficking across remote borders; to monitoring water flow from glaciers and water use downstream; or securing international events like the Nomad Games, there are huge opportunities for cooperative monitoring and security efforts with shared drone capabilities. 
Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Tajikistan don’t need Russia or China to address these challenges. They don’t need to depend on a foreign manufacturer for drones or the capabilities to produce many of the UAVs that have wide-ranging applications for the economy, environment, and defense of the region. And, to paraphrase some advice from Kenneth Waltz: they should be considering how to counterbalance new hegemonic threats, not swapping one vulnerability for another. Indeed, Astana is already headed in this direction.
The international order is being remade in real time, so regional governments need to look to their own security. Great powers might “ignore” their smaller neighbors for a time, but who’s to say when that benign neglect will come to an end. Investment in joint education, training, and production today can enable these states to address problems regionally, and sever dependencies at the same time, and make the whole region more secure from external threats over the long run. If they wait until the next regional conflict, it may be too late.
Drones are everywhere in the news and on the frontlines of the Iran-U.S. War and the Russia-Ukraine War, but their most recent use on a battlefield in Central Asia represents a long-term issue – continued dependency on foreign suppliers.
