articles.title: To Succeed in AI, South Korea Is Reinventing Its Developmental State Model
articles.full_text:
South Korea is betting big on universal AI access, using state activism and corporate collaboration to strengthen its position in the global AI race.
South Korea has embarked on an ambitious plan by launching the “AI for All” initiative, which aims to make artificial intelligence (AI) widely accessible to all its citizens. This initiative reflects a broader effort to integrate AI into almost every corner of Korean society. Rather than treating AI simply as another emerging technology, South Korea increasingly views it as a technology that will help realize its domestic economic development plans and geoeconomic objectives, retain its technological advantages in key strategic industries, and gain a strong foothold in emerging technologies amid intensifying technological competition.
The South Korean government plans to provide AI learning opportunities to approximately 5.14 million people in 2026. To support this initiative, it is developing AI services based on South Korea’s sovereign AI models, including a general-purpose AI chatbot that citizens will be able to use without charges or usage limits. More importantly, Seoul’s long-term ambition is to move toward an environment in which its citizens can have access to their own AI agents.
This plan can be understood as part of a broader trend among East Asian countries, particularly South Korea and China, toward emphasizing the rapid implementation and widespread application of AI. This approach reflects the distinction drawn by Kai-Fu Lee in his book “AI Superpowers: China, Silicon Valley, and the New World Order,” in which he contrasted China’s implementation-driven model with the innovation-first strategy associated with the United States. It also differs from the European approach, which places greater emphasis on AI governance, regulation, fundamental rights, and data privacy.
In many parts of the world, especially in liberal democracies, AI remains a subject of debate over safety concerns. In South Korea and other East Asian countries, however, the debate is different: it focuses on how rapidly AI can be deployed. The geoeconomic logic behind this approach is that rapid deployment will not only strengthen their positions in the AI ecosystem but also enable them to become future leaders.
South Korea views AI as one of the most promising next-generation growth engines and a strategic technology that will determine the country’s economic competitiveness. Seoul is learning from its historical experience, as the country’s growth has largely depended on technological upgrading and export-oriented manufacturing. Therefore, South Korea has linked AI to national survival, just as it did with semiconductors, which now form the backbone of the South Korean economy. South Korea’s strength in the semiconductor industry also supports its advancement in AI, as the expansion of AI is closely connected to growing demand in semiconductor-related sectors, including advanced memory, computing infrastructure, and AI chips.
The continuing legacy of developmental state practices in South Korea has generated a unique level of commitment among the state, businesses, and society to realizing the country’s national ambitions. Historically, South Korea’s rapid technological advancement resulted from the state’s long-term planning, the establishment of national targets and industrial strategies, businesses’ active support and compliance, and, most importantly, society’s largely unopposed embrace of rapid, growth-oriented development. This national consensus prioritizes technological advancement and the fostering of key strategic industries over other considerations. The same pattern can clearly be observed in the case of AI. 
In South Korea, political parties across the ideological spectrum support not only the rapid advancement of AI but also the goal of making the country a leading AI superpower. When the conservative government led by Yoon Suk-yeol was in power, South Korea set the ambitious goal of becoming one of the world’s top three AI powers, alongside the United States and China. The progressive government under Lee Jae-myung came to power in 2025 after Yoon was impeached, amid significant political conflict and turmoil involving conservative political forces. Nevertheless, one objective remained unchanged: South Korea’s national ambition to become a world-leading AI power. Therefore, a national consensus exists around realizing this ambition, regardless of changes in government and the high level of bipartisan political conflict within South Korea. That’s a consensus rarely seen in many liberal democracies.
The government’s ambition is also being reinforced by extensive business participation and, more importantly, growing societal demand for AI adoption. Frequent meetings between the government and business leaders are taking place in Seoul, with both sides agreeing that they must cooperate extensively to realize South Korea’s national ambitions. 
Even more important is the growing social demand for AI implementation in South Korea. The general view is that rapid deployment will enable society to adopt AI more quickly, ultimately creating new opportunities for both the public and the country. According to a recent survey, almost seven out of ten South Koreans believe that AI services, deployed in collaboration with the government and corporations, will positively impact society.
This contrasts sharply with debates in Western liberal democracies, where AI adoption is often discussed in terms of privacy violations, job displacement, and other risks. Moreover, state-led AI planning is often viewed with greater suspicion in societies where anti-statist attitudes are more widespread. This does not mean that such concerns do not exist in South Korean society. However, many people appear to place these concerns within the broader context of the national priority of technological advancement and the belief that South Korea should not fall behind in the global AI race.
In implementing its AI strategy, Seoul is deploying the practices of the developmental state, through which it previously achieved rapid technological advancement and built globally competitive strategic industries, including semiconductors and shipbuilding. Under this model, the state acts as a proactive planner, investor, and coordinator while collaborating closely with major domestic conglomerates.
Such practices are less common in neoliberal regulatory states, where proactive state intervention and close state–business collaboration – particularly with large corporations – are often viewed negatively. In South Korea, however, the state is actively fostering AI development in cooperation with major domestic companies. Meanwhile, many other countries, particularly liberal democracies, remain preoccupied with debates concerning AI regulation, oversight, and responsibility.
As a result, South Korea has moved far ahead in terms of large-scale investment in AI. While many parts of the world are waiting for, or heavily dependent on, private-sector investment in AI, the South Korean government is taking the lead in creating and expanding a substantial domestic AI market. One important example is South Korea’s decision to increase its national AI budget from 3.3 trillion won in 2025 to 10.1 trillion won in 2026 – almost three times the previous year’s allocation. This expansion occurred despite concerns about the country’s fiscal health. Such aggressive spending on a particular strategic industry also reflects South Korea’s developmental state philosophy of concentrating substantial resources on selected industries with high growth potential.
In addition to its investment role, the state is acting as a coordinator, which is another characteristic of developmental state practices. Under this model, state agencies play proactive roles as pilot agencies responsible for fostering strategic industries. For example, the Ministry of Science and ICT has been actively working with major conglomerates and other technology companies to establish consortia and accelerate AI development and implementation. This was evident in the ministry’s 2025 selection of five industry-led teams – Naver Cloud, Upstage, SK Telecom, NC AI, and LG AI Research – to develop sovereign foundation models. 
More recently, the ministry selected three consortia, led respectively by SK Telecom, KT, and Kakao, to operate the “AI for All” project. In both initiatives, the ministry has acted as a pilot agency coordinating public and private actors around national strategic objectives.
This extensive collaboration is not limited to ministerial-level coordination. The government is also providing financial and material support to foster public–private partnerships. For example, to accelerate the implementation of “AI for All,” the South Korean government will provide the three selected consortia with access to up to 512 Nvidia B200 GPUs. Moreover, the government will subsidize part of the expenses involved in developing and operating these AI services.
The government will also finance public access by supporting the provision of AI chatbots to citizens without subscription fees or usage limits. Above all, participating companies will gain access to public service systems, enabling them to connect their chatbots with public AI agents that provide services related to taxation, healthcare appointments, education, and government support programs. Such access has generally remained restricted for private companies in many other parts of the world.
The Global Implications of South Korea’s AI Strategy 
South Korea’s rapid deployment of AI across society offers several insights into the country’s political-economic approach to AI in particular and strategic industries more generally. By encouraging the widespread use of AI at an early stage, the government aims to create a large domestic market in which South Korean companies can develop, test, and improve their AI models, thereby supporting South Korea’s sovereign AI strategy. This approach strongly recalls the developmental state model that South Korea previously adopted to accelerate the growth of its strategic industries. 
Indeed, South Korea’s lead in AI deployment is driven by a geoeconomic logic through which it seeks to maintain its technological advantages and become an AI superpower. More importantly, it reflects the deployment of developmental state practices, with the state playing a pivotal role and fostering collaboration with South Korea’s major technology companies to realize its national ambitions. Equally significant is the broad societal support for this state-business nexus in AI development. This is a distinctive feature carried over from South Korea’s developmental state era and is once again visible in its approach to AI deployment.
Nevertheless, a major challenge remains: how South Korea will address its shortage of AI talent. If South Korea is able to overcome this challenge, we may witness the emergence of a new technological power in the global AI race alongside the United States and China.
South Korea’s efforts to become one of the world’s top three AI powers also have global implications. If South Korea continues to compete with the U.S. and China for a leading position in AI, it would not be surprising to see a large number of South Korean AI companies, alongside American and Chinese firms, emerge as dominant players in the global market. As seen in today’s semiconductor industry, where companies from a small number of countries dominate and control key technologies, we may similarly witness the emergence of an AI landscape in which companies from only a few countries exercise extensive control, while the rest of the world remains primarily on the consumer side.
South Korea’s rapid deployment of AI across society is likely to place it among the first group of countries. The actions taken today are likely to produce results for countries actively developing AI, in contrast to the more passive approach currently adopted by many others. It should therefore not be surprising if South Korea emerges as a global AI leader in the near future. 
South Korea has embarked on an ambitious plan by launching the “AI for All” initiative, which aims to make artificial intelligence (AI) widely accessible to all its citizens. This initiative reflects a broader effort to integrate AI into almost every corner of Korean society. Rather than treating AI simply as another emerging technology, South Korea increasingly views it as a technology that will help realize its domestic economic development plans and geoeconomic objectives, retain its technological advantages in key strategic industries, and gain a strong foothold in emerging technologies amid intensifying technological competition.

articles.title: China Is Moving Toward a New Form of Coercion at Sea
articles.full_text:
China is pushing patrols into new waters near Taiwan, regularizing its presence, and deploying research vessels that can conduct military reconnaissance.
Since Beijing announced special maritime operations on June 6, its forces have grown more assertive – pushing patrols into new waters, rotating formations to regularize presence, and deploying research vessels that can conduct military reconnaissance. This all points to a new form of coercion taking shape. 
On July 4, the Global Times – a mouthpiece for the Chinese Communist Party – declared that China’s maritime patrols had entered “a new phase,” defined by a move towards “a more systematic, institutionalized, and long-term framework” and away from “isolated military exercises or patrols.” 
Recent deployments bear this out. Between June 6 and June 10, China’s Ministry of Transport carried out its first special operation in waters east of Taiwan, halting commercial vessels and requesting information on their points of origin and destination.
While China has announced mandatory inspections during past exercises, it has never successfully enforced them. This time was different. Chinese Coast Guard ships conducted inspections en masse through radio communications with all transiting commercial vessels. Even foreign commercial vessels – including three vessels from Singapore, Benin, and Liberia – reported receiving radio messages from Chinese authorities to comply with requests.
According to Chinese state news agency Xinhua, across those four days, Chinese maritime authorities inspected 198 passing vessels, and even “rectified violations involving three ships.” The sheer quantity of reported inspections, followed by a public announcement of the results, demonstrates China’s ability to govern vessel traffic in Taiwan’s waters. Beijing uses that as grounds to assert jurisdiction over the island and to push the narrative that cross-strait dynamics are China’s internal affairs.
These operations may be testing grounds for an eventual quarantine, where China selectively permits commercial vessels to enter or leave, exerting immense pressure on Taiwan’s supply lines. If that is the case, the series of multi-day patrols serve two functions.
First, they test how foreign nations respond to maritime traffic controls. Knowing which nations elect to respond, and to what degree, gives Beijing some sense of what to expect. The United Kingdom, Germany, and France, for instance, issued a joint statement expressing alarm over the maritime activities. Australia raised concerns directly with Chinese officials. How forceful Beijing judges the pushback to be will affect the intensity of operations. In the event of an actual quarantine, though, responses are likely to be more pronounced. 
Second, they normalize China’s vessel inspections, shortening the leap to a quarantine. In July, China’s Coast Guard began rotating its formations to regularize its law-enforcement presence. The Global Times has noted the advantages of maintaining a “constant presence” because “a normalized presence itself exerts pressure.” The longer Beijing can keep ships on station, the more quickly it can impose a quarantine.
The location of operations is unusual as well. Until June, China appeared to prioritize the Taiwan Strait, where conditions are most favorable for launching an amphibious invasion. Oddly enough, the maritime operations have been concentrated in waters opposite the strait, to the east of Taiwan. The island’s eastern coast has long been regarded as a low-priority zone as steep mountains make military landings difficult.
But choosing to operate in the east is not random. The move effectively shrinks the space that Taiwan can operate in, aligning with China’s broader boa-constrictor strategy to sever the island from international support. More telling is that these patrols, China claims, were initiated as a response to talks between Japan and the Philippines to delimit maritime boundaries east of Taiwan. Beijing hopes to deter strategic cooperation between two U.S. allies, one located north and the other to the south of the island, that may each play critical roles during a conflict over Taiwan.
A final novelty of the recent operations is the sharp increase in Chinese research vessels operating in waters around Taiwan. While Beijing maintains that these ships only conduct marine scientific research, their missions appear far less benign. Publicly available tracking data shows that these vessels could be systematically mapping the undersea terrain, presaging planning for naval operations. Since June 6, at least seven research vessels have been suspected of conducting research with military applications.
Taken together, these signs indicate that a more intrusive form of coercion is taking form. Regional nations would be unwise to dismiss this as more of the same.

articles.title: Where Does North Korea’s Nuclear Program Stand in 2026?
articles.full_text:
Here’s what satellite imagery and the IAEA are telling us.
In this photo provided by North Korean state media, leader Kim Jong Un visits a new uranium enrichment facility on June 3, 2026..
Nearly two decades after international inspectors were expelled from North Korea, satellite imagery and open-source analysis remain the only windows the outside world has into Pyongyang’s nuclear program. What that window shows in late 2026 is a program that is visibly expanding, on multiple fronts at once.
On August 28, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) issued a report to its Board of Governors documenting the construction of a second uranium enrichment facility at North Korea’s main Yongbyon nuclear complex. The new facility could house up to 28 centrifuge cascades, alongside an already-operating expanded annex at the Kangson enrichment site. The agency identified the new two-story building by comparing satellite images taken during its construction with state media photographs of a June 2026 visit by Kim Jong Un, during which centrifuges and cascades resembling those at known enrichment sites were visible.
IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi told the Board that the continued operation of the Kangson and Yongbyon facilities, together with the reported further expansion of weapons-grade nuclear material production, was “a cause for serious concern.” The IAEA has not had inspectors on the ground in North Korea since 2009 and now builds its assessments entirely from commercial satellite imagery and open-source material, including North Korean state media itself.
The picture built up over 2026 by independent monitors is consistent with the IAEA’s findings. Analysts tracking Yongbyon have documented near-continuous water discharge from the 5-megawatt-electric (MWe) reactor, North Korea’s original plutonium producer, consistent with it running through what is now believed to be its seventh irradiation cycle since October 2024, alongside periodic steam activity at the Radiochemical Laboratory suggesting reprocessing campaigns. A separate site review by Daily NK reached similar conclusions, also noting that the long-delayed Experimental Light Water Reactor (ELWR) is showing renewed discharge activity after a shutdown period, and that demolition of the old, unfinished 50 MWe reactor at Yongbyon continues in parallel with the new construction.
A review by 38 North covering 2025 activity framed this as a direct response to political direction: Kim Jong Un had described that year as decisive for “bolstering up the nuclear forces,” and the satellite record showed the 5 MWe reactor running steadily since January 2025. 38 North also flagged pre-operational testing of the ELWR, a probable summer reprocessing campaign, and construction of what are assessed to be new enrichment and waste-storage buildings.
North Korea’s declared and suspected enrichment infrastructure now spans at least two locations at Yongbyon (the original uranium enrichment plant and the new building identified in August) plus the Kangson facility outside Pyongyang, whose 2024 annex expansion appears to have become operational around January 2026. Because clandestine centrifuge halls are comparatively easy to conceal, nonproliferation researchers have long argued that the more reliable way to bound North Korea’s enrichment capacity is to track its uranium supply rather than guess at hidden buildings. In 2021, an academic study using satellite-based land-use analysis around the Pyongsan uranium mill concluded that North Korea’s tailings output implies it could produce substantially more milled uranium than it is believed to currently be enriching, meaning supply is not the constraint on how fast the program could grow.
Unlike uranium enrichment, North Korea’s plutonium supply chain runs through a small number of well-mapped facilities. It starts at the Pyongsan Uranium Concentrate Plant, roughly 45 kilometers from the DMZ, which remains the country’s only confirmed source of yellowcake. Uranium ore is processed there into oxide concentrate before being shipped to Yongbyon for conversion into reactor fuel. That fuel feeds the 5 MWe reactor, whose spent fuel rods are then reprocessed at Yongbyon’s Radiochemical Laboratory to extract weapons-grade plutonium. This lab is believed to be responsible for the totality of North Korea’s plutonium stockpile to date, estimated by outside experts to support somewhere in the range of dozens of warheads.
The ELWR adds a second, more ambiguous track. Rated at 100 megawatts-thermal, it began sustained operation in late 2023 after a decade of delay. The ELWR has since gone through at least one documented shutdown-and-restart cycle, with Grossi telling the IAEA board of direction in November 2025 that it had “likely been shut down” in early August of that year, after months of stable running. As noted above, the ELWR is believed to have restarted once again.
A light-water reactor of this design is not optimized for weapons-grade plutonium production the way the graphite-moderated 5 MWe unit is, and North Korea has publicly framed it as an electricity source. Even so, should it reach stable, full-power operation, outside analysts assess it would function as a supplementary plutonium source layered on top of the existing reactor, meaningfully increasing Yongbyon’s total fissile material output.
The reactor most often described in older reporting as North Korea’s “second 200-megawatt reactor” is not at Yongbyon at all, but roughly 20 kilometers away at Taechon. Construction of this larger, 200 MWe graphite-moderated, gas-cooled unit began in the late 1980s as the planned full-scale successor to the 5 MWe design but was frozen under the 1994 U.S.-North Korea Agreed Framework, at which point North Korea had manufactured none of the reactor’s required graphite blocks). The most recent detailed satellite review of the site, by 38 North in 2019, found administrative and support-building upgrades but no changes to the derelict reactor structure itself or its generator hall. The analysts concluded that renewed construction was less likely than signaling or preparation for eventual inspections. No subsequent commercial satellite analysis has documented a resumption of reactor construction at Taechon; as of 2026 it remains, by all available open-source evidence, an abandoned shell.
The reason Taechon still draws attention despite decades of dormancy is the scale of what it was designed to do. At full design output, a 200 MWe graphite-gas reactor of this type could produce on the order of 220 kilograms of weapons-grade plutonium per year – enough, by some open-source estimates, for 25 to 40 additional nuclear weapons annually, dwarfing the output of the 5 MWe reactor that has anchored North Korea’s plutonium stockpile for four decades. 
In practice, most nonproliferation analysts consider a Taechon restart unlikely in the near term: the design is nearly 40 years old, the site has been exposed to the elements for three decades, and North Korea’s more recent investment has gone into the ELWR and centrifuge halls rather than graphite-gas technology. But the reactor’s unfinished shell, still standing, is a reminder that North Korea’s ambition for plutonium production was never defined by its current 5 MWe reactor. 
There are three main takeaways from open source analysis of North Korea’s nuclear program in 2026. First, North Korea is continuing a steady, uninterrupted plutonium cycle at the original 5 MWe reactor. Second, its light-water reactor has started on-again, off-again operation, which could add a second plutonium stream if it stabilizes. Finally, its uranium enrichment complex has now visibly doubled its footprint at Yongbyon while continuing to expand at Kangson. 
The fact that North Korea did all this without meaningfully touching the Taechon project tells us that Pyongyang has found it more efficient to build new capacity rather than revive old designs. That may be the most consequential inference to be drawn from Taechon.

In practice, most nonproliferation analysts consider a Taechon restart unlikely in the near term: the design is nearly 40 years old, the site has been exposed to the elements for three decades, and North Korea’s more recent investment has gone into the ELWR and centrifuge halls rather than graphite-gas technology. But the reactor’s unfinished shell, still standing, is a reminder that North Korea’s ambition for plutonium production was never defined by its current 5 MWe reactor. 
There are three main takeaways from open source analysis of North Korea’s nuclear program in 2026. First, North Korea is continuing a steady, uninterrupted plutonium cycle at the original 5 MWe reactor. Second, its light-water reactor has started on-again, off-again operation, which could add a second plutonium stream if it stabilizes. Finally, its uranium enrichment complex has now visibly doubled its footprint at Yongbyon while continuing to expand at Kangson. 
The fact that North Korea did all this without meaningfully touching the Taechon project tells us that Pyongyang has found it more efficient to build new capacity rather than revive old designs. That may be the most consequential inference to be drawn from Taechon.
articles.summary: Here’s what satellite imagery and the IAEA are telling us.

articles.title: How Looming US Sanctions Test India
articles.full_text:
The passage of the Lindsey Graham Act in the House and Senate allows President Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on exports from India to the US.
Reliance Industries Ltd.’s Jamnagar oil refinery in Gujarat, India.
On September 16, the U.S. House of Representatives passed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act with a 262 to 159 vote. The U.S. Senate had passed the legislation on August 7 with an overwhelming majority, which means that the bill now awaits only presidential approval.
Named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham, a staunch supporter of Ukraine, who spearheaded negotiations on the bill with the White House, the bill effectively allows President Donald Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on exports to the U.S. from the top five purchasers of Russian oil or natural gas, making exceptions for countries that import less than 15 percent of their natural gas from Russia and are taking “significant” steps to reduce the imports. Additionally, the bill provides for a range of sanctions against Russian officials and Moscow’s shadow fleet of vessels.
Following the bill’s passage, Senator Richard Blumenthal publicly remarked that China and India “better clean up” their “act” and buy oil and gas “somewhere else.”
As of August 2026, India was the second largest buyer of Russian oil, behind only China, leaving the two Asian giants most exposed to potential U.S. tariffs. Between December 2022 and August 2026, China accounted for 50 percent of Russia’s total crude exports, while India accounted for 37 percent.
India’s Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) was quick to issue a statement on the passage of the bill, stating that it had raised the issue with the U.S., highlighting its impact on “not just the bilateral relationship but also the international energy market.” It reiterated that New Delhi remains “committed to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people…..through diversified sourcing and on the basis of evolving market dynamics.” It also reaffirmed India’s determination to take “all necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests.”
The language and tone of India’s statement are notably different from its response last year, when Trump first announced “punitive” tariffs on Indian goods over Russian oil purchases on August 6, 2025. New Delhi had then explicitly called out Washington’s actions as “unjustified and unreasonable,” highlighting Western hypocrisy by pointing out that both the European Union and the U.S. continued trade with Russia. It also said that India would take all necessary measures to safeguard its “national interests and economic security,” linking the dispute with state sovereignty.
This time, the MEA dropped the word “national interest” entirely, focusing instead on “trade and economic interests.”
Rhetoric aside, the impact of Western scrutiny on New Delhi’s oil purchases is evident from the actions of major Indian refineries. By November 2025, India’s largest conglomerate, Reliance Industries, which owns the world’s largest and most complex oil refining hub in the world, announced that it would stop importing Russian crude oil for its exports. However, this proved to be short-lived as Reliance resumed buying Russian crude from December 2025.
State-controlled refineries such as Mangalore Refinery & Petrochemicals, Ltd., and HPCL-Mittal Energy Ltd also reportedly suspended Russian oil imports in the aftermath of the U.S. sanctions.
Meanwhile, in October 2025, India’s oil imports from the U.S. increased to 10.7 percent from around 3 percent earlier in 2025, while Russian oil imports decreased by 38 percent. By January 2026, India’s crude oil imports dropped to about 1.1 million barrels per day, down by 23.5 percent from December 2025 and by about a third compared to numbers from January 2025.
Correspondingly, the share of West Asian oil in India’s crude imports rose to 55 percent, its highest since late 2022, when India started buying Russian oil aggressively.
Such curbs proved to be short-lived as disruptions in West Asia, stemming from the U.S.-Israel war on Iran, created instability in energy supply chains in the region. Following a temporary U.S. waiver issued on March 5 this year — to allow the sale and delivery of sanctioned Russian oil which has already been loaded on vessels to India — India purchased around 30 million barrels of Russian crude. By July 2026, India’s imports of Russian crude reached a record high for the second consecutive month, rising by 2.1 percent month on month, 53 percent of which was transported by “shadow sanctions.” Global Trade Research Initiative data reveals that India bought $40.8 billion worth of Russian crude in FY 2026, accounting for 30.3 percent of its total crude imports.
In September 2026, amid the looming threat of U.S. tariffs, preliminary data suggests that Indian imports of Russian crude have already declined to about 30 percent lower than the August average of around 2.1 mbpd, according to data from trade intelligence firm, Kpler.
Historically, even when sanctions increased the logistical costs of shipping Russian oil, discounts offered by the Kremlin still made Russian crude commercially viable. Now, together with the looming threat of U.S. sanctions and narrowing discounts on Russian crude amid increasing Ukrainian attacks targeting refineries, New Delhi finds itself in a particularly difficult position.
Experts warn that replacing Russian crude with other suppliers will result in an increase in import bills, which would adversely impact the gross refining margins of the refining and marketing industry. This explains why many Indian refiners chose to return to purchasing Russian crude despite sanctions.
For New Delhi, caving in to the U.S. pressure will also have an adverse impact domestically and risk damaging ties with its “all-weather friend” Russia. As things currently stand, the only hope for New Delhi is pushing for the waiver option listed in the legislation, per which the President can waive the sanctions if it is “in the national interest of the United States.”
As talks with Washington over a free trade deal continue, New Delhi could potentially demand the waiver as part of the ongoing negotiations. The real challenge lies in identifying India’s sources of external dependencies vis-à-vis energy security and addressing them by building state capacity.

articles.title: Arrests and Court Appearances Heighten Political Tensions in the Philippines
articles.full_text:
What are the political implications of Martin Romualdez’s arrest, Rodrigo Duterte’s ICC appearance, and the new criminal case against Vice President Sara Duterte?
Philippine politics was anything but dull in the past two weeks.
During this time, an arrest warrant was issued against Vice President Sara Duterte, who immediately posted bail and called for the resignation of her erstwhile ally, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
Former House Speaker Martin Romualdez was arrested for plunder while recovering in a hospital before being transferred to a regular jail facility.
And lastly, former President Rodrigo Duterte made his first trial in-court appearance after more than a year of being under the custody of the International Criminal Court (ICC).
These high-profile events will continue to unfold and affect not just the Marcos presidency but also the narratives of the 2028 elections.
Sara Duterte’s arrest warrant was issued in relation to the grave threats complaint filed against her after she said in an online video in late 2024 that she hired someone to kill Marcos and his wife. She posted bail to avoid arrest and called out Marcos for being ungrateful and betraying those who voted for him.
Duterte minced no words against Marcos in a speech delivered in front of her supporters outside a local court: “You’re a liar, abusive. He has no debt of gratitude to our people and everyone who went to the precincts to put him in power. He has no shame.”
The case is distinct from the current impeachment trial against Duterte, although the first article presented by the prosecution also related to the threats made by the vice president against the First Family.
After the drama surrounding Duterte’s posting of bail, an anti-graft court ordered the arrest of Romualdez in connection with his role in the flood control kickback scandal. The arrest was cited by Palace supporters as proof that Marcos is seriously pursuing accountability, since Romualdez is his close ally and first cousin. Romualdez spent a few days in the hospital before being placed in a regular prison cell.
The arrest was also seen as a move to counter the claim of Duterte’s camp that the vice president, her family, and allies were being unfairly targeted by the Marcos government.
It was also timed a few weeks before the first anniversary of the massive anti-corruption protests that demanded accountability against all those implicated in the flood control controversy.
Arresting Romualdez was therefore a political necessity for Marcos to dispute the allegations that he was persecuting the Dutertes, boost the credibility of his government’s anti-corruption drive, and assure the public that there’s no let-up in pursuing cases against corrupt officials.
As a former House speaker, Romualdez was the highest official tagged in the corruption scandal. It could ease the pressure on Marcos, who is also accused of masterminding the anomalous budget insertions. It could divert attention toward Romualdez and his accomplices in Congress, and weaken the clamor to scrutinize the culpability of Marcos and other Palace officials in the rollout of corruption-tainted pork barrel projects.
Meanwhile, Duterte’s appearance at the ICC coincided with the presentation of evidence concerning his daughter’s alleged unexplained wealth in the ongoing impeachment trial.
What are the political implications of Sara Duterte’s case, Romualdez’s arrest, and Rodrigo Duterte’s ICC appearance?
Sara Duterte’s fiery speech after posting bail may be intended to consolidate her base, portray herself and her family as victims of political persecution, and enhance the prospects of her presidential candidacy. On the other hand, the case reflects their eroded political influence and signals to senator-judges sitting in the impeachment trial that the Marcos government is mobilizing all remedies to remove the vice president from her position.
Romualdez appears to be the Marcos government’s sacrificial lamb amid the continuing uproar against the unresolved corruption mess. Public vigilance is crucial to reverse the impunity that has plagued the country’s political system. A former Cabinet member of Marcos who was also charged with plunder was recently released after agreeing to be a witness. Imelda Marcos, the president’s mother, was acquitted this month by the Supreme Court in a 1991 case involving a portion of their alleged ill-gotten wealth. This is the reason why Romualdez’s arrest could not totally appease the public, who have become skeptical about the real agenda behind the decision to finally charge the president’s first cousin with a non-bailable plunder complaint.
Rodrigo Duterte’s surprise appearance at the ICC, after months of waving his right to attend the trial, has agitated his loyal following and could strengthen his family’s clout. But it also made it clear that he is finally being held to account for the bloody “war on drugs” during his term.
The recent political developments should not be reduced to a mere maneuver among political factions competing for dominance ahead of the 2028 elections. Marcos is evading accountability and desperately denying his lame duck status. Sara Duterte wants to survive the crisis that she herself created, but could not muster enough political support to hit back at Marcos. It is the people speaking out against corruption and protesting in the flooded communities that could sway the political balance and determine how the Marcos presidency will end in 2028. This is the crowd that embodied the anger against the corrupt budget system and demanded an end to political dynasties. They are not easily swayed by spectacles staged by political parties, and they can certainly make Philippine politics more interesting in the lead-up to the 2028 elections and beyond.

articles.title: Indian Navy Augments Its Submarine Rescue Capability
articles.full_text:
Commissioned on August 31, INS Nipun significantly augments the Navy’s specialist diving, underwater intervention, salvage, and submarine rescue support capability.
INS Nipun, which was commissioned on August 31, 2026.
On August 31, India commissioned INS Nipun, the second dedicated Diving Support Vessel (DSV) that serves as the mothership for the two Deep Submergence Rescue Vehicles (DSRVs) in service. With this, the Indian Navy crossed a threshold in a critical operational capability – submarine rescue – that has a bearing not just for India but for the entire region.
Submarines are some of the most complex machines in existence and their operation is highly specialized. Submarine rescue takes that to another level and is a forte of a very small group of countries.
Indian Navy Chief Admiral Krishna Swaminathan’s remarks at the commissioning ceremony in Mumbai aptly encapsulate this. The Nipun significantly enhances the capacity to respond to a distressed submarine, whether of the Indian Navy or that of a partner navy, he said, adding that this capability would also enable India to support submarine rescue and emerge as the “preferred submarine rescue partner” in the region.
The Indian Navy signed a deal worth 193 million British pounds (around $217 million) with U.K.-based James Fischer Defense in 2016 under which it procured two DSRVs, a Launch and Recovery System (LARS), and a LARS-integrated decompression chamber. They were operationalized at Mumbai on India’s western seaboard at the end of 2018 and at Visakhapatnam on the eastern seaboard in early 2019. Concurrently, in September 2018, the navy signed a deal with state-owned Hindustan Shipyard Limited, located at Visakhapatnam, for the construction of the two DSVs, with the first vessel to be delivered in 36 months.
Until the DSVs were completed, INS Sabarmati of the Ship Building Corporation of India acted as the interim ship for both the vessels. This left a major operational void, as it meant more time, which is the most critical factor in the event of a submarine disaster in the ocean depths.
The two vessels were launched into water in September 2022, and the first, INS Nistar, was commissioned on July 18, 2025. The induction of INS Nipun now closes that loop, significantly augmenting the Indian Navy’s specialist diving, underwater intervention, salvage, and submarine rescue support capability.
So far, the Indian Navy operated an older diving support vessel, INS Nireekshak, with limited submarine rescue capabilities. In the backdrop of the capability gaps in the past, India had signed an agreement with the United States for utilizing the U.S. Navy’s global submarine rescue flyaway kit.
Displacing 10,000 tons, measuring over 118 meters in length, and with an endurance of 60 days, the Nistar and the Nipun were purpose-built for deep-sea diving and underwater operations for inspection and intervention and to serve as mother ships to the DSRVs. Each DSV can accommodate 25 officers and 225 sailors.
Further, the expansive deep-sea diving systems with specialized diving complex, dynamic positioning capability, and associated life-support and medical facilities enable them to conduct sustained operations at sea, according to the Indian Navy. For this, they carry a 15-ton subsea crane, a diving bell, remotely operated vehicles (ROVs), side-scan sonar, compression chambers, and a self-propelled hyperbaric lifeboat. They can undertake deep-sea diving and salvage operations up to a depth of 300 meters.
The DSRVs, in turn, can go down to a maximum depth of 650 meters and rescue 14 people in one go. They also carry a ROV and, together with the side-scan sonar, can locate a submarine at depths of up to 1,000 meters. Once a submarine is successfully located, a sub-module of the system, the Submarine Rescue Vehicle, mates with the submarine to rescue trapped personnel. The same feature can also be utilized to provide emergency supplies to a submarine.
In 2018, before induction, the DSRV was put to trials, during which it set several “firsts” for the Indian Navy. It dived to a depth of 666 meters, the deepest submergence by a manned vessel in Indian waters, and carried out ROV operations at over 750 meters and side-scan sonar operations at over 650 meters.
Given the nature of its operation, the DSRV is designed for ease of transportation. For this purpose, the entire system has been divided into 24 components, which can be easily transported by road, sea, and air. In addition to being paired with the mothership, the system can also be airlifted by heavy transport aircraft like the IL-76 and C-17 operated by the Indian Air Force, enabling swift deployment across theaters.
Reaching a disaster-struck submarine in the narrow time window is critical and a DSRV offers that lifeline for any submarine-operating Navy. For the Indian Navy, the order of criticality multiplies manifold, given its aging submarine fleet.
The Indian Navy operates 16 conventional submarines – six Russian Kilo-class submarines and four German HDW-class submarines, both aging fleets long awaiting replacement, as well as six newer French Scorpene-class submarines. The newest Kilo-class sub is 26 years old, and the HDW class is over 30 years old. The fleets saw life extensions to keep them going amid delayed procurements. As stated by Captain Vikas Gautam, officer-in-charge of the Submarine Rescue Unit (East), during Exercise Milan in February this year, the true measure of any navy is not only its firepower, but “its resolve and capability to bring its men and women home safely.”
Regional Assistance and Cooperative Arrangements
The maritime domain with its wide expanse is inherently complex, and submarine rescue is a restricted capability both in terms of complexity and economics. In the last few years, India has signed several cooperation agreements with countries in the region for submarine rescue, offering its capabilities, which span bilateral arrangements and multilateral engagements.
The Indian Navy also actively cooperates with the International Submarine Escape and Rescue Liaison Office (ISMERLO), established by the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), which coordinates international submarine rescue responses.
In a demonstration of India’s capabilities in real time, in April 2021, India dispatched the two DSRVs to locate the missing Indonesian submarine KRI Nanggala, one with the mother ship and another airlifted in a C-17. However, they were recalled midway as the disaster-stricken submarine was located in the ocean depths. All crew onboard were dead.
In January 2021, India and Singapore signed an implementing agreement on submarine rescue support and cooperation between the two navies. In September 2024, India and South Africa signed an implementing agreement that ensures the safety of the South African Navy’s submarine crew in times of distress or accident.  In October 2025, during the visit of India’s Defense Minister Rajnath Singh to Canberra, India and Australia, which have transformed their maritime engagement over the last decade, signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on submarine search and rescue cooperation. A month later, in November 2025, India and Vietnam signed an MoU on mutual submarine search and rescue support.
Submarine rescue has also become a major part of bilateral and multilateral exercises, underscoring its importance. In September 2025, the Indian Navy deployed the Nistar for Exercise Pacific Reach (XPR-25), hosted by the Singapore Navy in the South China Sea, which saw the participation of over 40 nations. During this event, the DSRV Tiger X carried out its maiden dive outside the Indian Ocean Region (IOR) and achieved mating with South Korea’s submarine Shin Dol-Seok.
The Indian Navy also regularly showcases its submarine rescue capabilities at multilateral engagements it hosts, like the Exercise Milan and Goa Maritime Conclave, offering assistance to countries in the region.
As the IOR and beyond see a proliferation of submarines, their search and rescue in times of crisis will be much needed. India is now well positioned to lend immediate assistance, expanding the ambit of humanitarian assistance and disaster relief efforts.

articles.title: Indonesian Parliamentary Committee Debates Changes to Fiscal Deficit Limit
articles.full_text:
Some lawmakers say that the current administration should have the right to a 3 percent ceiling in order to support its expansive economic agenda.
Indonesian lawmakers have begun debating potential changes to the country’s fiscal deficit ceiling, with several ‌lawmakers arguing yesterday that President Prabowo Subianto’s administration should have the right to exceed the current limit in order to fund its ambitious welfare policies.
During a public hearing in Jakarta yesterday, the House of Representatives’ Commission XI debated a series of revisions of the State Finance Law. Passed in the wake of the Asian financial crisis of 1997-1998, the law sets a maximum budget deficit of 3 percent of gross domestic product and limits government debt to 60 percent of GDP.
Mukhamad Misbakhun, chairman of the House of Representatives’ Commission XI, told the hearing that the deficit limit should not necessarily be treated as a rigid annual threshold if the government needs additional fiscal space to support economic growth.
“Is 3% really ‘sacred’?” said Mukhamad, according to a report in the Jakarta Globe.
Misbakhun, who is also a lawmaker of the Golkar Party, a member of Prabowo’s expansive coalition, proposed that the law be revised to establish clear conditions under which a larger deficit could be permitted, such as when tax revenue is weak, or state energy subsidies rise due to a spike in global energy prices – as happened in Indonesia after the outbreak of the U.S.-Israel-Iran war earlier this year.
“We have the momentum to get out of the middle-income trap, ​take 233 million people out of middle income and head to high income,” Misbakhun said, according to Reuters. “That needs growth expansion. How ‌are ⁠we going to expand growth if we lock ourselves and always talk about 3 percent?”
Mohamad Hekal, deputy head of the committee and a member of Prabowo’s party Gerindra, agreed that changes to the budget deficit ceiling should be discussed.
While a deputy finance minister said yesterday that the government is committed to keeping the 3 percent ceiling in place, the ongoing parliamentary debates are likely to be watched closely by institutional investors.
The State Finance Law was passed in 2003, as Indonesia was pulling itself up from the economic rubble of the Asian financial crisis, the political reverberations of which brought down the three-decade-long reign of President Suharto.
As one scholar noted at the time, the law marked “a major step forward in Indonesia’s drive to establish a sound system of public finance management and realize good governance.” More importantly, perhaps, the law was intended to reassure foreign investors that the country would maintain a disciplined fiscal policy after the chaos and corruption of the late Suharto years.
The fiscal deficit rule has been largely unquestioned by Indonesian governments in the two decades since, but has come under scrutiny since Prabowo took office in October 2024. Shortly before his inauguration, reports emerged that the former general was exploring ways to raise the fiscal deficit and debt-to-GDP ratio ceilings in order to fund his ambitious policy agenda. This included a multibillion-dollar free lunch program, a broad defense modernization plan, and an ambitious target of 8 percent annual GDP growth across his five-year term.
The suggestion that Indonesia was preparing to loosen, or even do away with, these financial safeguards unsettled markets, as did Prabowo’s bull-headed and unilateral approach to economic management. In March, both Moody’s and Fitch announced ratings outlook downgrades for Indonesia, with the latter citing the “increasing ⁠policy uncertainty and erosion of Indonesia’s policy mix consistency and credibility” and the “growing centralization of policymaking authority.”
This has contributed to a high turnover of personnel atop Indonesia’s main economic policymaking institutions. This week, Prabowo fired his finance minister, Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa, just over a year after his appointment, and replaced him with his deputy. Purbaya himself was appointed after the removal of Sri Mulyani Indrawati, who had served as finance minister under three presidents, over disagreements about the direction of economic policymaking under Prabowo. July also saw the resignation of Perry Warjiyo, the governor of Bank Indonesia.
“If the deficit ceiling is indeed raised from the current 3 percent of GDP, a potential positive impact would be greater flexibility in financing government programs,” the local brokerage Phintraco Sekuritas said, according to the Jakarta Globe. At the same time, this could also increase government debt and affect the absorption of government securities and corporate bonds issued by private companies.
“Furthermore, global investors and international rating agencies could perceive Indonesia’s fiscal discipline as weakening, potentially triggering credit rating downgrades, capital outflows and rupiah depreciation,” Phintraco Sekuritas added.
However, not all members of the Commission agreed that the deficit limits should be tampered with. Harris Turino, a lawmaker from the Indonesian Democratic Party of Struggle, the only political party in parliament that is not a member of Prabowo’s coalition, said that it was important to keep the deficit ​ceiling in place.
“If we are unable to ⁠discipline ourselves, including in maintaining the 3 percent deficit limit, the market will eventually discipline us,” he told Reuters.

Mukhamad Misbakhun, chairman of the House of Representatives’ Commission XI, told the hearing that the deficit limit should not necessarily be treated as a rigid annual threshold if the government needs additional fiscal space to support economic growth.
“Is 3% really ‘sacred’?” said Mukhamad, according to a report in the Jakarta Globe.
Misbakhun, who is also a lawmaker of the Golkar Party, a member of Prabowo’s expansive coalition, proposed that the law be revised to establish clear conditions under which a larger deficit could be permitted, such as when tax revenue is weak, or state energy subsidies rise due to a spike in global energy prices – as happened in Indonesia after the outbreak of the U.S.-Israel-Iran war earlier this year.
“We have the momentum to get out of the middle-income trap, ​take 233 million people out of middle income and head to high income,” Misbakhun said, according to Reuters. “That needs growth expansion. How ‌are ⁠we going to expand growth if we lock ourselves and always talk about 3 percent?”
Mohamad Hekal, deputy head of the committee and a member of Prabowo’s party Gerindra, agreed that changes to the budget deficit ceiling should be discussed.
While a deputy finance minister said yesterday that the government is committed to keeping the 3 percent ceiling in place, the ongoing parliamentary debates are likely to be watched closely by institutional investors.
The State Finance Law was passed in 2003, as Indonesia was pulling itself up from the economic rubble of the Asian financial crisis, the political reverberations of which brought down the three-decade-long reign of President Suharto.
As one scholar noted at the time, the law marked “a major step forward in Indonesia’s drive to establish a sound system of public finance management and realize good governance.” More importantly, perhaps, the law was intended to reassure foreign investors that the country would maintain a disciplined fiscal policy after the chaos and corruption of the late Suharto years.
The fiscal deficit rule has been largely unquestioned by Indonesian governments in the two decades since, but has come under scrutiny since Prabowo took office in October 2024. Shortly before his inauguration, reports emerged that the former general was exploring ways to raise the fiscal deficit and debt-to-GDP ratio ceilings in order to fund his ambitious policy agenda. This included a multibillion-dollar free lunch program, a broad defense modernization plan, and an ambitious target of 8 percent annual GDP growth across his five-year term.
The suggestion that Indonesia was preparing to loosen, or even do away with, these financial safeguards unsettled markets, as did Prabowo’s bull-headed and unilateral approach to economic management. In March, both Moody’s and Fitch announced ratings outlook downgrades for Indonesia, with the latter citing the “increasing ⁠policy uncertainty and erosion of Indonesia’s policy mix consistency and credibility” and the “growing centralization of policymaking authority.”

articles.title: Why Is Thailand Not Prosecuting Members of the Mauerberger Network?
articles.full_text:
One year after the South African national Benjamin Mauerberger and his network were first exposed, not one intermediary has been charged.
Benjamin Mauerberger, a South African national allegedly involved in financial networks connected to online scamming operations in Cambodia.
On their Whale Hunting blog in August 2025, Tom Wright and Bradley Hope began exposing the vast financial network built by the Cambodian businessman Yim Leak and the South African Benjamin Mauerberger, known in Bangkok as Ben Smith. In May 2026, the U.S. House Select Committee on China published a bipartisan report, “Crime, Corruption, and Power.” The report claims that a “South African fixer” is alleged to have operated between Cambodia’s crime hubs, developers linked to the Chinese Communist Party, and Thailand’s elite economy, laundering enormous illicit proceeds into Thai markets. All three footnotes cite Wright and Jacob Sims, a visiting fellow at Harvard University who specializes in Southeast Asia’s scam economy.
Thailand appears in that report twice. The first mention of the country is as a victim of the regional scam economy, with domestic losses put above 115 billion baht ($3.5 billion) a year, according to a 2025 estimate by Global Anti-Scam Alliance. The second is the market where many of the profits from Southeast Asian scam centers come to rest. By my own count, those proceeds sit in more than 20 listed and unlisted Thai companies, in holdings worth over 26 billion baht ($778 million). Thailand has become rather good at finding this money, but it has not begun to prosecute the people who helped to move and launder it.
The revelations have implicated a sitting member of the government. Vorapak Tanyawong, a former president of Krungthai Bank, was appointed deputy finance minister on September 19 of last year. He resigned 33 days later, after Whale Hunting reported that he had once been listed as an adviser to Cambodia’s BIC Bank, whose chairman is Yim Leak, and alleged that his wife had received $3 million in cryptocurrency from a Chinese-Cambodian criminal network. Vorapak, who has not been charged with any offence, has denied all of it. He said he had met Yim Leak but never advised or worked for BIC, called the reporting a smear campaign, and announced he would sue for defamation.
I should disclose where I stand. I am a former investment banker who has spent the past year documenting this network’s footprint in Thai capital markets on my blog, fringer.co. Vorapak is the plaintiff in the criminal defamation suit I am currently defending. I have also received cease-and-desist letters from Chartered Group, Capital Asia Investments, and others connected to them. And I now advise the parliamentary committee trying to extract answers from the regulators.
So here is my scorecard for the Thai agencies involved, ranked from best to most disappointing.
The Anti-Money Laundering Office deserves praise. Two orders, in December 2025 and April 2026, provisionally froze 102 items worth roughly 20.4 billion baht ($610 million). This included shares in listed companies including Bangchak Corporation and Finansia X, securities accounts, cars, loan claims, and a yacht. These are temporary seizures, not forfeitures, and the parties can petition the court to get the assets back. By Thai standards, it is still remarkable work.
The Department of Business Development has moved against illegal nominees, and the Central Investigation Bureau has broken up scam compounds and traced laundering routes through Cambodia-based Huione Pay. Huione Pay’s parent company Huione Group was severed from the U.S. financial system in October 2025 due to its alleged role as a “critical node” for laundering proceeds from transnational crimes and scams. In February 2026, the bureau obtained arrest warrants for Mauerberger and his Thai wife, Cattaliya Beevor.
These warrants deserve a closer read, however. They rest on an alleged investment fraud dating to 2016, in which one foreign investor claims losses of more than 1 billion baht. The money-laundering counts attached are predicated on that private fraud, not on the scam-compound proceeds. Mauerberger is reported to have left Thailand last September, and his lawyer has described the case as a civil dispute over a share purchase agreement.
Which brings me to the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). In July 2026, the parliamentary committee sent it 20 questions, asking for each to be marked done, in progress, or not started, with a timeline. The six-page reply answered one question, on new know-your-customer guidelines, directly. It used the phrase “currently under examination” six times, and attached a deadline to none of the 20 questions. It did not once mention the efforts of Singapore’s police and central bank, who in March arrested two directors of Capital Asia Investments (CAI), and froze more than S$160 million. CAI is the fund manager behind several of the committee’s questions about potential securities law violations that the SEC should duly investigate.
What it has produced instead is enforcement at the edges. In June, it referred Finansia Syrus Securities to police over deficiencies in client identification; in July and August, it also referred Yim Leak to police over shareholding disclosures filed late or not at all. One of those included a finding that he was the beneficial owner of a fund that crossed 5 percent in the advertising company VGI. These are not insubstantial, but amount to mere filing offences.
The substantive questions remain unanswered. In August 2025, a rights offering lifted CAI’s stake in the brokerage group Finansia X from 24 percent to 44 percent without triggering a mandatory tender offer. The top four shareholders hold about 64 percent between them. And in April this year, Alpha Chartered Energy, whose stake in the energy company Bangchak Corporation AMLO was frozen in December, was permitted to vote at Bangchak’s annual meeting on a bylaw amendment written to exclude shareholders in exactly its position. The amendment failed. What exactly is the SEC waiting for?

Concealed control of listed companies, undisclosed acting in concert, and share issues structured to avoid tender-offer obligations are all offences under Thailand’s Securities and Exchange Act. Third, the government needs to publicize its findings. Currently, the authorities are going after convenient individuals at awkward moments while the structure generating the revenue keeps running.
Next month, Bangkok will host the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank for the first time since 1991. Finance ministers and central bank governors will spend a week in a country that has frozen 20.4 billion baht of assets tied to this network and charged nobody with helping to move them. Thailand has six weeks to show that it is finally willing to go after the local enablers.

articles.title: Why Malaysia Won’t Extradite Dr. Zakir Naik to India
articles.full_text:
Despite being wanted on various criminal charges in India, the Islamic preacher has become hugely popular since arriving in Malaysia in 2016.
Dr. Zakir Naik, as seen in a screenshot of a video posted to his YouTube channel on Aug. 22, 2025.
The biggest viral video of the recently concluded BRICS Summit in New Delhi was not of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi shaking hands with Chinese President Xi Jinping, but of Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim singing a Hindi film song.
At a gala dinner during the summit, Anwar spotted a pianist in the hotel lobby and started singing Kishore Kumar’s evergreen “Khwaab Ho Tum Ya Koi Haqeeqat” from the 1965 Dev Anand film, “Teen Deviyan.” Indian movies are very popular in Malaysia, and Anwar must have grown up listening to Bollywood songs because he has sung this song many times on past visits to India.
But once the music stopped, Anwar returned to serious business, and one issue he must have been aware that every Indian journalist would ask him about was the extradition of Islamic preacher Dr. Zakir Naik.
Naik, who faces multiple criminal charges in India relating to hate speech, inciting terrorism, and money laundering, moved to Malaysia in 2016 and has remained there since. India formally sent an extradition request to Malaysia in January 2018. New Delhi has also sought an Interpol Red Notice for Naik’s arrest. Interpol declined India’s request citing that the request was premature because a formal charge sheet had not been filed at the time of the original application.
Anwar handled the issue with due maturity, given that the extradition of Naik is a deeply sensitive domestic political issue. He confirmed that the matter had been discussed with Modi but avoided making any commitment on handing Naik over. Malaysia, he said, had to proceed cautiously and respect the rule of law and the importance of bilateral relations.
India and Malaysia have an extradition treaty, signed in 2010, but Naik’s case is different. Malay Muslims constitute more than 70 percent of the country’s population, and no party can afford to offend them. And since arriving in Malaysia, Naik has become very popular among Malay Muslims. At times, many political parties, especially Barisan Nasional, have used the issue of Naik to shore up political support among hardline Muslims.
Naik claims he has been persecuted in India because of his faith and will never get a fair trial if he is extradited.
“No Malaysian government will extradite him as he has a large following among the Malay Muslims and secondly, it will be seen as anti-Islam and that Malaysia, being a Muslim nation, failed to protect a fellow Muslim,” said Arfa’eza Abdul Aziz, a Kuala Lumpur-based communications consultant.
This is the reason why neither Najib Razak, Mahathir Mohamad, nor Anwar can even think of extraditing Naik. The issue has become more complicated because, like Mahathir’s second-term government, the present Anwar government also has the Democratic Action Party (DAP) as a coalition partner. The DAP, which is dominated by Malaysian Chinese, makes any government in which it is a part vulnerable to accusations of being anti-Malay or anti-Islam.
Mahathir was more blunt when he said in June 2019 that Malaysia would not deport Naik if he didn’t break any of Malaysian law.
Apart from his popularity among Muslims, Naik’s biggest support comes from Islamist groups, including the opposition Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party (PAS). PAS had earlier warned of political backlash if Naik was deported.
In 2019, the New Straits Times quoted political analyst Mohamed Mustafa Ishak as saying that Malaysia was shouldering a huge responsibility to protect a fellow Muslim, regarded as a renowned scholar, from harm.
“Zakir Naik is neither a terrorist nor has he been proven to have links to related (terrorist) networks,” he said.
Mustafa, who is also an expert in ethnic relations in Malaysia, warned of a dire outcome should Kuala Lumpur accede to India’s request.
“There will be a huge protest among Muslims not just domestically, but all over the world,” he said.
The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) under Prime Minister Modi has hardly helped its case. The BJP’s 12-year rule has seen Muslims being lynched in the name of cow protection, while many Muslim leaders and activists have been languishing in jail for years without trial. In Uttar Pradesh, a state ruled by the hardline Yogi Adityanath, the so-called bulldozer rule has seen houses of Muslims demolished on the pretext of protests or offering prayers outside their homes. The deletion of millions of names from voter lists has further added to the concerns. There is hardly any sign that the Modi government is softening its stringent stance towards Muslims.
Given this situation, the issue of Naik’s extradition appears to have been effectively shelved.

articles.title: Former Philippine President Duterte Makes First In-person Appearance at ICC
articles.full_text:
The physical state of the 81-year-old raised questions about his fitness to participate in what is likely to be a protracted trial.
Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte attends a status conference at Trial Chamber III at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, Netherlands, Sep. 16, 2026.
Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte appeared in person at the International Criminal Court (ICC) for the first time on Wednesday, ahead of his trial for atrocities committed during his violent “war on drugs” campaign.
Duterte, 81, has been in the court’s custody since his arrest in the Philippines in March 2025. He faces three charges of crimes against humanity for extrajudicial killings carried out during the anti-drug campaign, a flagship policy of his administration between 2016 and 2022.
For all of the pre-trial hearings so far, including his initial appearance in March 2025, Duterte has appeared via video link from the ICC’s detention unit.
He appeared yesterday before the ICC’s Trial Chamber III, which held a third status conference to discuss how to manage the sprawling case against Duterte. The Inquirer.net reported that the case involves “hundreds of thousands of pages of documents, more than 1,000 audio and video files, and an estimated 193 hours of direct examination by prosecution witnesses.”
During the proceedings, Duterte sat quietly sipping water and at one point stood and waved to family ​members in the public gallery, Reuters reported.
However, the physical condition of the former president, who appeared thin and haggard, raised the question of whether he will live to see a verdict – and whether he is even fit to stand trial.
Duterte’s attorneys claimed last year that he was in frail health and that his condition was deteriorating in the ICC’s detention unit. In one filing in June, they argued that the ex-president’s illness and “advanced age” created “compelling humanitarian grounds” for judges to grant his interim release. In September 2025, they claimed that he was unfit to stand trial due to “cognitive impairment in multiple domains.”
In January, judges rejected the defense claims, arguing that Duterte “is able effectively to exercise his procedural rights and is therefore fit to take part in the pre-trial proceedings.” They also requested his physical presence in court.
However, the defendant’s advanced age and apparent ill-health are likely to remain pressing issues as the court moves toward the beginning of his trial on November 30.
At Wednesday’s hearing, Presiding Judge Joanna Korner expressed concerns about the volume of evidence and the length of the prosecution case. She said the chamber was “very anxious” that the prosecution case should conclude “as swiftly as possible in the circumstances,” due to Duterte’s age and health. The trial is set to ​begin on November 30.
“It’s important this trial goes ahead as quickly as possible,” ​she said, pressing parties to limit the number of witnesses and focus on key evidence.
Duterte’s attorney, Peter Haynes, said that his team did not have the time to examine the tens of thousands of pieces of evidence submitted by prosecutors, calling the task “enormous ⁠and impossible.”
“If I had a younger and healthier client, I would request pushing back the trial by six months,” he said, as per Reuters.
Duterte is charged with the murders of at least ⁠76 people and the attempted murder of two ​others. Nineteen of the alleged murders were carried out between 2013 and 2016, when Duterte was mayor of Davao City. The remainder were committed during the “war on drugs” campaign, which Duterte launched upon becoming president in 2016. The campaign resulted in a death toll of at least 6,000 – the official estimate of the Philippine police – but independent estimates run as high as 30,000.
In April of this year, the ICC’s Pre-Trial Chamber I confirmed the charges against Duterte and ordered the case to go to trial. The chamber’s judges concluded that “there are substantial grounds to believe that Mr. Duterte is responsible for the crimes against humanity of murder and attempted murder.” These crimes “were committed as part of a widespread and systematic attack against a civilian population on the territory of the Republic of the Philippines.”
The alleged crimes took place between November 1, 2011, and March 16, 2019, the date on which Duterte withdrew the Philippines from the ICC’s Rome Statute.
