articles.title: Kazakhstan Again Sentences Activists for Supposed Attempt to Seize Power
articles.full_text:
Human rights organizations are speaking out after five Kazakh activists were convicted for an alleged plan to seize the presidential residence in Astana.
On September 8, five men were sentenced to between five and five-and-a-half years in prison after standing trial in an Almaty courtroom for supposedly attempting to seize control of power in Kazakhstan last year. The judges found all five suspects guilty not only of advocating for the violent seizure of power, but also of organizing mass unrest against authorities in the country and a seizure of the presidential residence, known as Akorda.
Several of the convicted have a past in activism, having taken part in multiple civil protests in the country over the years. While doors were closed for the hearings, the case sparked some attention from both activists and national human rights organizations. Along with criticizing the verdict, focus was also given to similar cases that had targeted activists previously. These types of court cases, activists argue, are part of a strategy employed by the Kazakh government to control opposition in the country.
While all of the defendants, aged between 56 and 62, were found guilty of advocating for mass riots and the seizure of power in Kazakhstan, two were found to have committed additional offenses. Kaisar Ozbek and Talgat Ashirov were convicted of illegally acquiring and storing explosives in relation to the unrest. These charges originally led the state prosecutor to request eight years in prison for each of the defendants.

She further criticized the decision to let the trial run behind closed doors, citing concerns for the rule of law: “They [the courts] don’t want transparency. They want to quickly shut everyone down without any fuss.”

articles.title: Siddhant Kishore on BRICS and the New Geopolitics of Asia
articles.full_text:
Siddhant Kishore joins host Tushar Shetty to examine the BRICS summit in New Delhi and the strategic realignment underway across Asia.
In this episode of Beyond the Indus, Siddhant Kishore, a New Delhi and Washington D.C.-based national security and foreign policy analyst, and former analyst at the Institute for the Study of War, joins host Tushar Shetty to examine the BRICS summit in New Delhi and the strategic realignment underway across Asia. 
They discuss the consensus preserved in the New Delhi Declaration and India’s diplomatic win on Pahalgam, the tactical stabilization between New Delhi and Beijing and why it falls short of realignment, the costly Iran-U.S. stalemate and Washington’s undefined war aim, the Houthi advance on the Bab al-Mandeb and the reconstitution of Iran’s proxy network, the operational hollowness of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, and the hedging by U.S. allies as Washington’s security commitments turn conditional.
For more in-depth analysis on South Asia, subscribe to the Beyond the Indus podcast on Spotify or Apple Podcasts, or follow us on YouTube for video episodes.

articles.title: What Is Hinduism?
articles.full_text:
Hinduism may not be as well-defined and creedal as Christianity or Islam, but it is not a meaningless label either. It refers to a real idea.
The Galtaji Temple, important to Vaishnavite Ramanandis, is located near Jaipur, India.
Earlier this month, Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS), a Hindu denomination that holds that an 18th-century yogi is the supreme manifestation of God-as-Krishna, stirred controversy in France recently.
It emerged that female staff at the Eiffel Tower were replaced by male colleagues during a visit by BAPS monks, who take a strict vow to not have any contact with women. During the uproar that ensued, many Hindu commentators argued that BAPS was not even Hindu, although the denomination says it is, and its massive temples are presented as Hindu.
The question of whether a denomination or sect is Hindu or not can arise because Hinduism itself can be a porous concept. The question of how to define Hinduism and who counts as Hindu has been the subject of vigorous debate for over two centuries. It is a question with political, spiritual, and legal — Indian personal law operates on the basis of an individual’s religion — ramifications.
The definition of Hinduism has emerged as an issue because, unlike Christianity or Islam, Hinduism does not have a single creed or canonical scripture. Modern Hinduism contains a large number of strands and traditions, some of which are quite at odds with each other.
Despite the extraordinary antiquity of many of these traditions, some scholars believe that a conception of Hinduism as a single, world religion emerged in the 19th century when the British colonial government constructed Hinduism to make sense of indigenous beliefs and categorize the population of British India that did not belong to other bounded, creedal religions such as Christianity and Islam. This process began with the first British census in India in 1872, which sought to enumerate and describe India’s religious groups and castes in great detail, thus entrenching communal classifications.
There is also a contemporary political angle to the debate on the origins of the idea of Hinduism. In his book, “Unifying Hinduism: Philosophy and Identity in Indian Intellectual History,” scholar Andrew Nicholson noted that the motivation of some thinkers “to assert that Hindu identity is purely a nineteenth-century colonial construction is to weaken Hindu communalism. For if ‘Hinduism’ is merely an artificial construction that outsiders imposed on Indians in the nineteenth century, simplistic historical narratives of medieval Hindu unity in the face of Muslim oppression would be proved false.”
However, an ideological approach to a field of study could distort objective assessments of the truth. In modern India, it has become all too commonplace to attribute every undesirable phenomenon, from lack of development, to caste, to communalism, to the British in order to strengthen one’s political argument.
The argument that Hinduism is a modern construction is based on observing its theological and ritual diversity. While the constituent parts of modern Hinduism include a number of ancient traditions, some going all the way back to the Vedic era over three millennia ago, those traditions often saw themselves as competitors. For example, the rivalry between medieval Vaishnavism and Shaivism — denominations who believe that either Vishnu or Shiva is the supreme god — is well-documented. Perhaps, in other circumstances, Vaishnavism and Shaivism would have been classified as separate — though related — religions, like Christianity and Islam.
Moreover, ancient India was home to a number of philosophical schools, which both interfaced with popular religion and asserted a number of metaphysical, ethical, psychological, and soteriological positions that were often at odds with one another. These schools, which included Buddhism, Jainism, Carvaka (materialism), and six systems now considered to be astika or orthodox Hindu philosophies, were often bitter rivals who engaged in polemical arguments. These schools held metaphysical positions that were starkly at odds with one another, and would, to a bystander, sometimes seem to be different religions. For example, Advaita Vedanta holds the position of radical monism — everything is literally of one principle, Brahman, which is also pure consciousness — while another school, Samkhya, proposes the opposite, that there is a complete duality between matter and consciousness, which is present in an infinite number of individuated souls. Samkhya, and another school, Mimamsa, are atheistic and posit that there is no creator god or ground of reality. The Yoga and Nyaya schools, however, posit a creator deity distinct from creation. Meanwhile, Vedanta’s god manifests as the world.
Thus, some scholars, such as the Indologist Paul Hacker, argue that Hinduism is a collective, descriptive label, just like Chinese folk religion.
There is, however, evidence for an alternative viewpoint, which holds that Hinduism was not simply fabricated by the British out of a random set of indigenous beliefs. Rather, Hindus developed a self-conception of their own tradition, one that took shape over time and sharpened vis-à-vis Hindu contact with Muslims and Europeans. Many elements of Hindu identity and self-conception are too deeply rooted for them to be explained simply as the outcome of a foreign census project lasting a mere century.
Hindus began to understand themselves first in ethnic and cultural terms before also coming to see themselves in religious terms. Hinduism never became a creedal, bounded religion with a single doctrine or set of scriptures, but Hindus did recognize, over time, a unity to their religion and a set of customs and rituals that characterized their tradition and separated it from other traditions.
The cultural element is reflected in the terminology used even in antiquity, which refers to groups that we would today call Hindus as arya or followers of the Vedas — ancient Hindu scriptures — and counterposes them with foreign groups with different practices: mlecchas (barbarians), Sakas (Scythians), Yavanas (Greeks), Turushkas (Turks), and others. According to Andrew Nicholson, by the medieval era, Hindus recognized a clear difference between themselves and other groups, a distinction that Muslim rule sharpened, because Hindus could clearly see the difference between their customs and those of Islam.
This is expressed in vernacular literature, such as the works of Kabir and the Marathi poet Eknath, whose writings refer to the differences between Hindus and Turks, or Muslims, including the differences in their modes of worship and theology.
Around this time, the term Hindu began to appear in inscriptions by Hindu dynasties, which used the term to characterize their rule as opposed to rule by the mlecchas or Turushkas. Some rulers of the Vijayanagara Empire (1335-1646 CE) called themselves “Sultan among Hindu kings.” The Maratha ruler Sivaji (1630-1680 CE) also self-consciously set up a “Hindawi” state, though with the caveat that this meant rule by natives of India as opposed to “Turks.” Nonetheless, it contained many clear Hindu ritual elements and the increased use of Sanskrit in place of Persian. Thus, Hindu ethnic identity began to crystallize even before the British period.
More importantly, starting in the late Middle Ages, Hindu scholars and philosophers began to conceptualize it as a single theological system. This was facilitated by the triumph of Vedanta and its partial absorption of the other Hindu philosophical systems. Despite their differences, the six orthodox systems of Hindu philosophy are rooted in a common Vedic tradition and agree on some principles, such as the existence of a soul as well as the cycle of rebirth and the aim of moksha (liberation) from this cycle. This is, in fact, essentially the definition of Hinduism given by the Supreme Court of India in its famous 1966 ruling Sastri Yagnapurushadji And Others vs Muldas Brudardas Vaishya And Another. The court asserted:
…underneath [the] divergence [of Hindu views] lie certain broad concepts which can be treated as basic, and there is a kind of subtle indescribable unity which keeps them within the sweep of broad and progressive Hindu religion. The first among these basic concepts is the acceptance of the Vedas as the highest authority in religious and philosophic matters. This concept necessarily implies that all the systems claim to have drawn their principles from a common reservoir of thought enshrined in the Vedas.
These commonalities, along with the loss of much political power amongst Hindus after the 12th century CE, blunted much of the rivalry between Hindu schools. Individuals like the 16th-century philosopher Vijnanabhiksu synthesized the Hindu philosophical traditions. For example, he advocated Yoga as a means to achieve the goal of liberation as set forth in Vedanta. He also understood the Samkhya division of matter and consciousness as two elements of a great whole, as understood by Vedanta. Other scholars approached synthesis from other angles, but the end results were generally similar, building upon earlier Hindu thought that held the various deities to be facets of one divinity.
This unity of Hindu schools and traditions deepened throughout Muslim rule and into the British colonial era. Thus, the British did not have to invent Hinduism out of whole cloth as a native understanding of what it was had already emerged. It was not simply a catch-all for indigenous traditions because it explicitly did not include Buddhist and Jain traditions, which rejected the Vedas and explicitly disagreed with the Hindu systems on the nature of the soul and goals of life. Hinduism may not be as well-defined and creedal as Christianity or Islam, but it is not a meaningless label either. It refers to a real idea.
Nonetheless, a great many traditions, including many with divergent viewpoints and practices, are indeed considered Hindu today, including the Swaminarayan sect that gave rise to BAPS. This is because followers of that group advocate a theology rooted in Vedanta of the philosopher Ramanuja and seek moksha through the worship of Krishna as manifested in their guru, Swaminarayan.
Earlier this month, Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS), a Hindu denomination that holds that an 18th-century yogi is the supreme manifestation of God-as-Krishna, stirred controversy in France recently.

During the uproar that ensued, many Hindu commentators argued that BAPS was not even Hindu, although the denomination says it is, and its massive temples are presented as Hindu.

articles.title: BRICS 2026: A Forum, Not a Front
articles.full_text:
Xi and Putin in Delhi made the headlines. The declaration tells the real story of India’s multi-alignment and why Europe should welcome it.
Much of the global attention on the BRICS Summit 2026 focused on the presence of Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in New Delhi. Given the photographs of the pair with the summit’s host, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, observers might find it tempting to cast the gathering as the meeting of an anti-Western bloc. That view may make for catchy headlines, but it risks missing how India sees the grouping and what value it brings even to its Western partners.
For New Delhi, BRICS is not a camp or a bloc, but a forum – one of several – that it uses to secure a seat at one of the tables defining the unfolding multipolar order. The evidence is in the declaration the leaders adopted and, above all, in what it leaves out.
The summit convened in a three-theater world full of uncertainties, where great power contest is playing out simultaneously in Europe, the Middle East, and East Asia. In the current interregnum – between the old and the new order – countries are navigating multiple developments and their consequences at once. The war in Ukraine is in its fifth year. The Strait of Hormuz has been closed to normal ship traffic for more than six months, ever since American and Israeli strikes on Iran in February. As a consequence, the Brent crude price, which touched $126 in March, is back above $100. The two superpowers – China and the United States – are actively working to secure their edge in energy, semiconductors, computing power, and critical minerals, which will underpin artificial intelligence and the next industrial era. Supply chains, which have been global in the past, are now being rerouted to adjust for political exposure; export controls and tariffs are being put in place and weaponized; payment systems are splitting. Additionally, defense budgets are growing. 
In such a world, India, a country of 1.4 billion people, cannot simply pick a camp to align with. Instead, it works with different power centers without allowing one relationship or grouping to determine all of its strategic and economic choices. That is what Indian officials mean by multi-alignment.
And what a year of multi-alignment it has been. India concluded a free trade agreement with the European Union and signed a security and defense partnership in the same week. Shortly afterwards, Delhi hosted the AI Impact Summit and struck a tariff truce with U.S. President Donald Trump without allowing it to dent the larger strategic relationship with the United States. India’s navy has escorted tankers through the Strait of Hormuz. It has a signed trade deal with the United Kingdom, officially entered into a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement with Oman, and signed a landmark free trade agreement with New Zealand, among other things. Now, India also is holding the BRICS chair. Each seems to be an active hedge against a different type of failure. 
None of these actions, however, is a sign of alignment. India is not looking to choose between the West and the rest. It is trying to create strategic space for itself. India may not have been looking to use the BRICS Summit to bring all members closer together, but rather to identify issues on which there is enough common ground to keep all members together and build consensus.
When reading the BRICS New Delhi Declaration, many things are mentioned, but some important issues are not named. The declaration does not mention the Strait of Hormuz. It doesn’t specifically mention Iran – except in echoing its bid for accession to the WTO – or the United States. It does not name Ukraine or the U.S. dollar. Even the largest disruption to the world’s energy supply appears only to be framed as the “continued escalation of tensions in Middle East/West Asia,” which should be met with “maximum restraint.” The grouping continues with a hope for the “smooth flow of global trade, supply chains and energy.” The tell is the phrase “recalling our respective national positions.” This is diplomatic language for saying that members could not agree and instead wrote around their differences.
India, as chair, seems to have been working around members’ quarrels and different perspectives. Countries such as Iran or Russia would presumably have pushed for stronger wording and a condemnation of U.S. action in Iran. Saudi Arabia and the UAE might have had a different opinion, having spent the summer intercepting Iranian drones. The host country, meanwhile, is engaged in ongoing negotiations with Washington and would have wanted a nuanced, neutral paragraph. The tariffs were mentioned only in one paragraph and former headline-making topics such as a BRICS currency are essentially nowhere. Further expansion of the grouping, too, seems to be off the table for now.
So it is fair to assume that India’s BRICS chairmanship was less about turning the grouping into a political front and more about finding the narrow but complicated areas of consensus that could hold a deeply diverse membership together.
Then there was Xi Jinping, who has not been to India in seven years. Ever since the 2020 border clashes, highlighted by the bloody fighting in Galwan Valley, India has seen China as an existential challenge to its national security, and the relationship took a turn for the worse. Modi’s meeting with Xi last year in Tianjin at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit and the latter’s visit to New Delhi this year have led to whispers about a strategic warming between the countries, mostly in the wake of the unpredictable policies of the Trump 2.0 administration. But some 50,000 troops remain on either side of their contested border, facing each other across the Line of Actual Control. During last year’s India-Pakistan conflict, Chinese support for Pakistan was crucial. In New Delhi, this is seen as collusion and strong military support for the country’s neighbor.
India is therefore talking to China not because it has decided that the rivalry has suddenly ended, but because it has decided to treat competition as a built-in feature of the bilateral relationship. Permanent rivalry needs mechanisms – especially given China’s size, the 3,488-kilometer border with India, its strategic weight and role in the multipolar world and the economic vulnerabilities New Delhi faces. Modi told Xi in Tianjin last year that their relationship “should not be seen through a third-country lens.” This can be understood as a rebuke to Beijing, which reads India’s ties with Washington as containment. But it applies with equal force to Western capitals interpreting India’s ties with Beijing (or the BRICS) as evidence that India is joining the China-Russia bloc.
The message from New Delhi is fairly consistent: engagement is not alignment, and managing rivalry is not the same as ending it.
The Indian-European relationship, meanwhile, is strong not just because of the recently politically concluded FTA and other frameworks, but because both sides are now actively building strategic trust. Economically, India is not a replacement market but a hedge against the geopolitical fragility driving the European economic crisis and features strongly in European “China+1” discussions. Every handshake between Russian, Indian, and Chinese decisionmakers triggers a debate in European capitals over which “camp” India belongs to – the West or an anti-Western front? It triggers fears of losing newly built, robust ties with one of the most decisive actors in a changing global order. 
These fears, however, are too binary and based on a limited misunderstanding of what makes India a valuable partner in the first place. For Europe, India is essentially a hedge against a fragile alliance system, an order that is breaking down and an increasingly less globalized economy. But such a hedge can only work if the respective partner is itself hedging. Imagine an India that had picked a camp: it would be a much smaller India without Russian energy, capital from the Gulf, its Global South connections, and the ability to balance Russia and China within the same grouping. The India in which Europe is investing is, by definition, the India that does all of the above – a country whose leaders take those handshakes.
The strategic trust in which both sides are heavily investing means seeing a partner as it is: being realistic about its capabilities, limitations, imperatives and trade-offs. India will not align itself with anybody, nor would this necessarily be a good thing for Europe. India wants a seat for its 1.4 billion people and a stake in the global order currently being rewritten. Europe wants India to have that seat. But it also wants a strong India to sit in rooms that Brussels cannot access itself. This is ultimately the value of India’s multi-alignment for Europe.
A stronger India with relationships across Washington, Moscow, Beijing, the Gulf, and the Global South is not against European interests but what makes India useful as a strategic partner in an increasingly fragmented world. That was the BRICS Summit 2026: a forum, not a front. For Europe, India is a partner worth having precisely because it refuses to align itself with anybody.

It has a signed trade deal with the United Kingdom, officially entered into a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement with Oman, and signed a landmark free trade agreement with New Zealand, among other things. Now, India also is holding the BRICS chair. Each seems to be an active hedge against a different type of failure. 
None of these actions, however, is a sign of alignment. India is not looking to choose between the West and the rest. It is trying to create strategic space for itself. India may not have been looking to use the BRICS Summit to bring all members closer together, but rather to identify issues on which there is enough common ground to keep all members together and build consensus.
When reading the BRICS New Delhi Declaration, many things are mentioned, but some important issues are not named. The declaration does not mention the Strait of Hormuz. It doesn’t specifically mention Iran – except in echoing its bid for accession to the WTO – or the United States. It does not name Ukraine or the U.S. dollar. Even the largest disruption to the world’s energy supply appears only to be framed as the “continued escalation of tensions in Middle East/West Asia,” which should be met with “maximum restraint.” The grouping continues with a hope for the “smooth flow of global trade, supply chains and energy.” The tell is the phrase “recalling our respective national positions.” This is diplomatic language for saying that members could not agree and instead wrote around their differences.
India, as chair, seems to have been working around members’ quarrels and different perspectives. Countries such as Iran or Russia would presumably have pushed for stronger wording and a condemnation of U.S. action in Iran. Saudi Arabia and the UAE might have had a different opinion, having spent the summer intercepting Iranian drones. The host country, meanwhile, is engaged in ongoing negotiations with Washington and would have wanted a nuanced, neutral paragraph. The tariffs were mentioned only in one paragraph and former headline-making topics such as a BRICS currency are essentially nowhere. Further expansion of the grouping, too, seems to be off the table for now.
So it is fair to assume that India’s BRICS chairmanship was less about turning the grouping into a political front and more about finding the narrow but complicated areas of consensus that could hold a deeply diverse membership together.
Then there was Xi Jinping, who has not been to India in seven years. Ever since the 2020 border clashes, highlighted by the bloody fighting in Galwan Valley, India has seen China as an existential challenge to its national security, and the relationship took a turn for the worse. Modi’s meeting with Xi last year in Tianjin at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit and the latter’s visit to New Delhi this year have led to whispers about a strategic warming between the countries, mostly in the wake of the unpredictable policies of the Trump 2.0 administration. But some 50,000 troops remain on either side of their contested border, facing each other across the Line of Actual Control. During last year’s India-Pakistan conflict, Chinese support for Pakistan was crucial. In New Delhi, this is seen as collusion and strong military support for the country’s neighbor.
India is therefore talking to China not because it has decided that the rivalry has suddenly ended, but because it has decided to treat competition as a built-in feature of the bilateral relationship. Permanent rivalry needs mechanisms – especially given China’s size, the 3,488-kilometer border with India, its strategic weight and role in the multipolar world and the economic vulnerabilities New Delhi faces. Modi told Xi in Tianjin last year that their relationship “should not be seen through a third-country lens.” This can be understood as a rebuke to Beijing, which reads India’s ties with Washington as containment. But it applies with equal force to Western capitals interpreting India’s ties with Beijing (or the BRICS) as evidence that India is joining the China-Russia bloc.
The message from New Delhi is fairly consistent: engagement is not alignment, and managing rivalry is not the same as ending it.
The Indian-European relationship, meanwhile, is strong not just because of the recently politically concluded FTA and other frameworks, but because both sides are now actively building strategic trust. Economically, India is not a replacement market but a hedge against the geopolitical fragility driving the European economic crisis and features strongly in European “China+1” discussions. Every handshake between Russian, Indian, and Chinese decisionmakers triggers a debate in European capitals over which “camp” India belongs to – the West or an anti-Western front? It triggers fears of losing newly built, robust ties with one of the most decisive actors in a changing global order.
articles.summary: Xi and Putin in Delhi made the headlines. The declaration tells the real story of India's multi-alignment and why Europe should welcome it.

articles.title: Underwater Autonomy in the China-US Naval Race
articles.full_text:
The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Verineia Codrean – chief strategy and partnerships officer at EUROATLAS, the Bremen-based company building the world’s longest-endurance autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV), GREYSHARK – is the 526th in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”
Explain why the China-U.S. naval race may increasingly depend on who controls the underwater operating landscape.
I would use the word “understands” rather than “controls.” No country can fully control such a vast and difficult environment. But the side that can map it, monitor activity persistently, communicate underwater, and turn sensor data into decisions faster will gain a significant operational advantage. The underwater landscape affects submarine movement, anti-submarine warfare, mine warfare, and the security of critical infrastructure, so situational awareness below the surface is becoming central to maritime power.
How might China’s expanding underwater reach undermine U.S. maritime dominance?
Greater underwater reach can complicate U.S. and allied operations by making submarines, ports, sea lanes, and critical infrastructure harder to protect. Persistent sensing and autonomous systems could extend surveillance over much larger areas and increase uncertainty for an opponent. But reach alone does not equal dominance: effectiveness depends on sensor quality, communications, data fusion, logistics, and the ability to operate reliably in complex environments.
In what ways is Taiwan a preview of deniable, below-threshold disruption in the China-U.S. naval race?
Taiwan illustrates the difficulty of distinguishing accidents, commercial activity and deliberate coercion at sea. Cable damage, vessels operating under flags of convenience, ambiguous ownership, and activity near sensitive infrastructure can create disruption without producing immediate, conclusive attribution. That ambiguity is strategically useful because it delays both political and operational responses. However, individual incidents should not be presented as deliberate state action unless the evidence supports that conclusion.
Analyze why underwater autonomy is becoming crucial for detecting, monitoring, and attributing threats below the surface.
The central problem underwater is persistence. Ships and crewed aircraft can only monitor limited areas for limited periods, while fixed sensors cannot cover every route or depth. Autonomous systems can extend presence, revisit anomalies, and collect data over time. That helps distinguish a one-off event from a pattern of behavior and can strengthen attribution. But autonomy does not solve attribution by itself: evidence still has to be combined with vessel tracking, acoustic data, intelligence and legal assessment.
Assess the top three trends in underwater intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance and their implications for risk management in maritime chokepoints, such as the Taiwan Strait, Strait of Malacca, and Strait of Hormuz, among others.
One important geographic distinction I want to highlight is that the risk is not identical across all chokepoints. The Taiwan Strait is primarily shaped by military and grey-zone competition; Malacca combines strategic rivalry with extreme commercial density; Hormuz combines state confrontation, energy security, and asymmetric threats. The technology may be similar, but the rules for interpreting and responding to an underwater contact must differ.
Underwater advantage will not belong simply to the country with the most platforms. It will belong to the side that can maintain persistent awareness, interpret ambiguous activity, and turn reliable data into proportionate decisions fastest.

articles.title: China’s Free-Trade Offer to Africa Won’t Solve the Trade Imbalance
articles.full_text:
Beijing has opened its enormous market to African exports. Whether that helps the continent move up global value chains is another question.
In Abuja on August 14, 2026, nearly 500 government officials, diplomats, scholars, and business representatives gathered for a seminar on China’s new zero-tariff policy and what it means for African economic transformation. Nigeria’s minister of state for agriculture, Aliyu Sabi Abdullahi, used the occasion to strike a cautious note. “Zero tariffs alone do not guarantee success,” he told the room. “The question before us, therefore, is not, can Nigeria export more? The question should be, can Nigeria export better?”
Since May 1, China has extended zero-tariff treatment across 100 percent of tariff lines to the 53 African countries with which it holds diplomatic relations. That gives nearly all of Africa (with the lone exception of Eswatini) duty-free access to one of the world’s largest consumer markets. The early results look encouraging: Chinese imports from Africa reached $28.7 billion in May and June, up 23.5 percent from a year earlier. During the seminar in Abuja, China’s ambassador to Nigeria reported that Chinese imports from Nigeria specifically had already grown more than 40 percent year-on-year in both May and June.
African governments have good reason to welcome China’s new zero-tariff policy. The problem is that lower tariffs alone cannot resolve the deeper imbalance that has built up in Africa-China trade.
Africa-China merchandise trade hit a record $348 billion in 2025, but the flows were badly lopsided. China sold Africa $225 billion in goods, Africa sold China $123 billion. For every dollar of goods Africa sold China, it bought back roughly $1.83. The resulting deficit, $102 billion, was 64.5 percent above 2024’s figure. In the same period, Chinese exports to Africa grew 25.8 percent, while African exports to China grew just 5.4 percent. 
Market access – like China’s new offer to African countries – can change the volume of trade, but not necessarily the structure of trade. What is actually being exported by each partner matters more than the size of the deficit itself. Research from the Boston University Global Development Policy Center and the African Economic Research Consortium found that from 2000 through 2022, 89 percent of African exports to China came from extractive industries: oil, copper, iron ore, alumina. Over the same period, 94 percent of African imports from China were manufactured goods. 
A 2026 update from the same researchers showed that not much had changed. Extracted natural resources still dominate Africa’s exports to China, while agriculture and manufacturing each account for a small share of export value. 
Most African countries have clearly stated ambitions to move up the value chain. Lower tariffs alone will do little to accomplish that goal. The rising volume of Africa-China trade is easy to measure and just as easy to celebrate, but the overall numbers are less important than the composition of trade. 
The tariff opening still matters, of course. African exports of avocados, apples, and oranges to China have risen sharply since implementation. Market access of this kind can pull real investment toward certification, cold-chain logistics, and packaging, some of the obstacles holding producers back. But that won’t happen automatically.
Take copper as an example. Copper can be exported from Africa as raw ore, or it can be refined and worked into components before it ships. Currently, that work – and the added value – happens almost entirely outside the continent. China’s zero-tariff policy doesn’t care whether the copper is raw or refined; the tariff line is the same either way. 
Two recent examples show what greater processing and value capture inside Africa can actually look like. At a processing plant in Kenya’s Athi River Export Processing Zone, locally grown avocados are ripened, sorted, and cold-pressed into extra virgin avocado oil bound for China. In Rwanda, a company that began exporting dried chilies to China in 2022 shipped its first batch of pickled chilies in June – a deliberate move toward a higher-value semi-processed product made only after the tariff change. In both cases, more processing is happening before the goods leave the continent, which means more of the value is captured in Kenya and Rwanda rather than downstream in China.
African countries do have the capability to move up the value chain, and intra-Africa trade proves it. UNCTAD reported that 61 percent of trade happening within the continent consists of processed and semi-processed goods, far above Africa’s share of processed exports to the rest of the world. The opportunity is to pair China’s external market with the regional value chains the African Continental Free Trade Area is meant to build. Cotton grown in Mali or Burkina Faso can be baled and shipped directly to China for processing, or it can move first through mills in Cote d’Ivoire or Ghana and leave as finished cloth.
It’s not tariffs that are holding back African manufacturing. China’s zero-tariff policy won’t solve problems like unreliable electricity, expensive financing, inefficient ports, thin transport links, certification bottlenecks, or customs delays. UNCTAD estimated that road transport alone accounts for about 29 percent of the price of goods traded within Africa, compared with 7 percent for goods traded beyond it. According to UNCTAD, non-tariff barriers constrain intra-African trade roughly three times more than tariffs. 
African governments need to treat China’s opening as one input into a larger industrial policy, not as a substitute for having one. Africa-China trade will likely keep setting records, but that alone won’t help African economies climb global value chains. The real test will show up in the breakdown of those trade statistics: whether Africa is still mostly exporting raw materials like crude oil and copper ore or refined metals and finished goods.

articles.title: Will Southeast Asia Actually Benefit From Its AI Boom?
articles.full_text:
Southeast Asia might end up hosting substantial computing capacity without developing a correspondingly deep AI economy.
Headlines have for years been touting the emergence of Asia as a global powerhouse in data center development. The nature of headlines is that all too often they prove to be horrendously wrong in the long or even the short run – but when it comes to data centers in Southeast Asia, they are repeatedly getting validated. 
The Asia-Pacific’s data center development pipeline reached a record 26.5 GW in the first half of 2026. Southeast Asia accounts for roughly half of the capacity under construction: Malaysia leads with 1,039 MW, followed by Thailand with 859 MW. 
All this investment is producing a division of labor among national markets: Singapore concentrates on high-value, power-constrained activity while Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Vietnam are absorbing different forms of large scale growth. 
The question is not whether Southeast Asia will add more data centers. It undoubtedly will. The more pressing question is whether the infrastructure being built across separate national markets could become the foundation of a regional AI economy.
Numbers of course, matter still. They always will. But not all numbers tell the exact same story. Under construction figures, for example, do not describe current operational capacity. At about 1.46 GW, Singapore retains the largest operational base in Southeast Asia, but its new capacity remains tightly controlled. Limits on power, land, and sustainability all but ensure that the country is unlikely to compete with its neighbors simply by adding volume. 
Instead, these constraints strongly favor higher value uses including premium workloads and research compute while reinforcing Singapore’s status as the region’s high trust, highly connected high tech hub, supported by its strengths in talent development, governance, research, and connectivity.
It’s of little surprise, then, that Singapore’s second Data Center Call for Applications and plans for a low-carbon park on Jurong Island both point toward increasingly selective, high specification projects rather than an expansion bonanza. On August 21, the government provisionally awarded 200 MW to four data center operators out of more than 20 applications. This latest and all too predictable display of Singapore’s constraints is bound to gradually push more investment across the Causeway.
Indeed, on the other side of the Johor Strait, Malaysia has emerged as the region’s leading scale market. More available land and comparatively lower costs combined with supportive industrial policy are attracting facilities designed for hyperscale operations and AI training workloads. 
Thailand, by contrast, had been expanding from a smaller base, with investment approvals and partnerships with domestic power producers supporting rapid growth particularly around Bangkok.
Indonesia and Vietnam illustrate another approach in which domestic market size and questions of digital sovereignty matter alongside foreign investment. Indonesia is pairing the region’s largest domestic market of about 288 million with large foreign AI projects while still requiring government and other designated strategic data to stay onshore. CoreWeave’s planned 360 MW deployment in Greater Jakarta illustrates how the country is moving from a primarily domestic-demand story toward a major destination for foreign AI infrastructure investment. Meanwhile Vietnam, home to 102 million people, has sought to attract investment through regulatory liberalization, including allowing wholly foreign owned data centers.
Capital, as it tends to, is moving across national markets, potentially enabling workloads to be distributed according to different national advantages, and constraints in one country increasingly affect investment decisions in its neighbors. As a consequence, instead of viewing them as isolated national opportunities, investors increasingly view ASEAN markets as complementary locations within a broader infrastructure strategy. 
On August 1, SoftBank’s Singapore subsidiary signed a memorandum of understanding with SC ZEUS, a Singapore-based data center developer, and Robust HPC, a Malaysian high-performance computing specialist, to develop AI data-center capacity focused initially on Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Vietnam.  
However logical it might be, this cross-border approach also exposes a problem. Instead of removing physical constraints, moving investment across borders redistributes them. Both Malaysia and Thailand are now facing limits in grid connections, transmission capacity, and the speed at which new power can be delivered. 
In early September Thailand asked developers to halt work on about 49 projects under construction and froze approvals for about 117 until it finalizes national rules on power, water, siting and local benefit. In Johor, the Malaysian state bordering Singapore, water supply has also been under pressure. 
Neither Bangkok or Kuala Lumpur are in a unique place. The United States, which accounts for approximately 45 percent of global data center capacity, is struggling to connect new load to the grid as demand continues to rise. Although energy generation potential is crucial for data center developers, it is far from being the only factor: whether firm power can reach the right location on the required timetable is equally, if not more, important. 
The ASEAN Power Grid seeks to make cross-border electricity trade more practical. An early example of what such a broader regional system could look like is offered by the Laos-Thailand-Malaysia-Singapore Power Integration Project, Rest assured, greater regional power connectivity will not eliminate local shortages or transmission bottlenecks, but it could give governments and developers a larger geography over which electricity supply and demand can be balanced. For an industry where expansion is increasingly constrained by access to reliable power, this matters almost as much as the movement of data.
As data centers spring up across the region, a thornier question is also taking shape: what do countries actually capture from all this infrastructure? Data centers bring construction. They bring engineering jobs, energy investment, and tax revenue. They also bring ceremonial ribbons to cut at opening ceremonies. But much of the higher-value activity associated with AI lies elsewhere: software, model development, research, specialized services and the use of AI across domestic industries. 
This is similar to a country hosting large electronics assembly operations without capturing the design, chip-making, or software layers that creates most value. Southeast Asia might end up hosting substantial computing capacity without developing a correspondingly deep AI economy.
Hence the terms attached to investment matter a lot. Governments can use access to land, power, and incentives to seek commitments on local skills, research partnerships, supplier development, and access to computing for domestic firms. Keeping foreign operators out should not be the objective. Instead, governments should put the wider AI value chain in their sights by turning data centers from isolated capital projects into anchors for broader technology ecosystems. Data centers should bring skills, suppliers, research capacity, and firms that can continue to create value after the next generation of facilities is installed.
The first challenge is domestic: ensuring that infrastructure investment produces capabilities rather than merely capacity. The second is regional: ensuring that those capabilities and services can operate across borders. Success will not come easily. The SIJORI (Singapore-Johor-Riau) Growth Triangle’s almost four-decade-long history shows that such cooperation may progress at a snail’s pace, and the path is marked by friction and incomplete results aplenty. 
While infrastructure is already becoming more geographically distributed, the rules governing its use remain largely national. A company may therefore place servers in various ASEAN countries while having to navigate different requirements for data governance, cybersecurity, licensing, and the cross-border provision of digital services in each market. 
There is also a very real risk that infrastructure fragments faster than regulation can connect it. If this happens, the region could end up with growing computing capacity without capturing the economic advantages of regional scale. Facilities would primarily serve national markets, companies would duplicate functions across jurisdictions, and firms seeking to operate regionally would face higher compliance and operating costs.
ASEAN’s Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA) may help to address part of this problem. Its scope extends beyond digital trade to areas including cross-border data flows, electronic payments, data protection, talent mobility, AI, and cybersecurity. Those areas are directly relevant to whether computing capacity located in one ASEAN country can support firms, services and users in another.
Naturally, DEFA cannot integrate the physical infrastructure itself. It cannot build transmission lines or address water shortages. Nor can it determine where data centers should be licensed. What DEFA can do is reduce some of the regulatory friction that makes a regional digital economy expensive to operate. Southeast Asia will need both forms of integration: physical connections for power and networks, and common or interoperable rules for data, services, talent and digital commerce.
Two months after signing DEFA, Singapore will assume the 2027 ASEAN chairmanship. The opportunity is ripe for the country to push not only for the agreement’s formal adoption but, in order to reduce cost of operation across the region, for practical implementation as well. 
National ambitions for greater control over AI and data will obviously not disappear in an instant, nor should they. But regional integration does not require governments to surrender control over sensitive infrastructure or information. Instead, it requires common rules and interoperability for countries to retain that control while still capturing the economies of regional scale.
The goal should be to turn infrastructure investment into skills, research capacity, local suppliers, and wider AI adoption. These capabilities should regionally be able to reinforce one another: a company operating in one country, computing capacity located in another, and electricity supplied through a wider regional grid need not function as entirely separate national systems.
Ultimately, gigawatts are a crucial yet imperfect measure of success. They make superb headlines, but the real measure is what they enable the region to do next. Bringing infrastructure to various regional countries is hard. But the more difficult challenge is to make national systems work together at a regional level, requiring governments, investors, and ASEAN institutions to ensure that, instead of operating in isolation, projects developed in various countries complement one another. The November 2026 signing of the Digital Economy Framework Agreement followed by Singapore’s 2027 ASEAN chairmanship will show whether policy can catch up with the infrastructure that is rapidly taking shape.
Headlines have for years been touting the emergence of Asia as a global powerhouse in data center development. The nature of headlines is that all too often they prove to be horrendously wrong in the long or even the short run – but when it comes to data centers in Southeast Asia, they are repeatedly getting validated.
articles.summary: Southeast Asia might end up hosting substantial computing capacity without developing a correspondingly deep AI economy.

articles.title: South Korea Embraces the Silk Road Spirit With Central Asian Leaders
articles.full_text:
In the first Central Asia-South Korea leaders summit, energy and critical minerals were top of the agenda.
Amid their first leader-level summit, South Korea and the five Central Asian states set a course for deeper relations centered on critical minerals, energy, and emerging technology, with a focus on seeking out mutual benefits and climbing the value chain together. 
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung called for the forging of a “new Silk Road.”
“If we walk together, I am certain that the road of 1,500 years ago will reopen as a new and beautiful Silk Road,” Lee said. “If the five countries gathered here today and we in the Republic of Korea pool our wisdom and join hands, there is nothing we cannot achieve together.”
On September 16 in Seoul, Lee met with the presidents of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan together for the first time, taking advantage of the C5+1 format that has become an increasingly popular vehicle for external powers to engage with the Central Asian region. 
Since 2007, Central Asian and South Korean officials have met at the vice-ministerial level, upgrading to the ministerial level in 2019 and now the presidential level. 
South Korea has long been an important partner for the region, though it flies under the geopolitical radar homed in on Russia, China, and the United States. Although the Central Asian states are marginal trade partners for South Korea, whose GDP of approximately $1.93 trillion makes it the 15th largest globally, Seoul is a top-10 trade partner for Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan. That trade, however, is often heavily weighted in South Korea’s favor, as in the case of Tajikistan – according to the Observatory of Economic Complexity (OEC), in July 2026 South Korea exported $31.6 million in goods to Tajikistan (mostly cars and other vehicles) and imported $0. 
For Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, the balance is better and the trade volumes bigger. In July 2026, OEC data stated, South Korea exported $158 million in goods (mostly cars and other vehicles but also beauty products) to Kazakhstan and imported imported $142 million (mostly crude petroleum, coal, and ferroalloys). In regard to Uzbekistan, South Korea exported $182 million in goods (mostly cars and other vehicles, as well as vehicles parts, but also – and I confess I don’t understand – $21.1 million in the “brochures” category); Uzbekistan meanwhile sent $7.06 million in goods (refined petroleum, perfume plants and medical instruments) to South Korea. 
In his remarks, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev highlighted Kazakhstan’s leading place in Central Asia-South Korea trade – representing half of it – and the prevalence of well-known Korean companies in Kazakhstan.
“More than 1,000 joint ventures with Korean capital operate in Kazakhstan,” he said. “Leading companies such as Kia, Hyundai, Doosan, Posco, Samsung, Lotte, and Hanwha have been successfully operating in the Kazakhstani market for many years.”
“There is significant potential in the industrial sector that requires further deepening economic cooperation,” Tokayev added. He made the case for further Korean investment in Central Asia, taking advantage of expanding trade and transit corridor across the Eurasian landmass.
Tokayev proposed launching a Central Asia-Korea industrial and technological development partnership. “Within this framework, our governments could create a portfolio of flagship joint projects with a focus on localization of production, technology transfer, development of regional cooperation, and export of finished products to third-country markets,” he added.
Meanwhile, Uzbekistan’s President Shavkat Mirziyoyev had his own proposals, mirroring those of Tokayev, including for a Central Asia-Korea Industrial and Technological Park
Energy and critical minerals – the former always in vogue and the latter the hottest topic at present – naturally received intense attention. 
On the energy front, conditions are not ideal but ambitions remains. “We are prepared to expand cooperation in this area, including resuming energy supplies to Korea,” Tokayev said. Recurring attacks on Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) infrastructure in recent years (and problems in the Red Sea in past years) have hassled and occasionally halted exports. About 80 percent of Kazakhstan’s oil exports pass through the pipeline system that carries Kazakh crude from the country to Russia’s Novorossiysk port, on the Black Sea. 
Critical minerals are the crux of nearly every conversation with Central Asian states these days, with external powers interested in what Central Asian can provide and regional governments keenly aware of both the opportunity at hand and the risks.
Mirziyoyev commented, “Today, Central Asia is no longer just a supplier of raw materials.” That may be putting the cart before the horse, but highlights regional ambitions to move up the value chain when it comes to critical minerals. 
“Given the rapidly growing demand for this valuable raw material and its vast reserves in Central Asia, the region is capable of becoming a leading supplier on the global market. Korea’s advanced technology and capital can play a decisive role in this,” Mirziyoyev said. He proposed a “Regional Investment Alliance for Critical Minerals.”
“Remarkably, all 10 minerals classified by Korea as strategic are present in our country’s mineral resource base,” Tokayev said, pitching Kazakhstan’s resource wealth. “The combination of Kazakhstan’s resource potential and Korea’s technological capabilities opens up broad prospects for mutually beneficial cooperation.”
Lee, in his remarks, spoke right to the heart of Central Asian ambitions. If trade at present is dominated by Korean cars and Central Asian oil, both sides are looking to what’s next. 
“We now need to move beyond these items and expand the scope of trade into new industries, including consumer goods, biotechnology, and digital sectors,” Lee said. He added, “As global supply chains are being reorganized, Central Asia is emerging as a treasure trove of critical minerals essential for the production of electric vehicles, batteries and semiconductors.”
The summit ended with a declaration – the Seoul Declaration – charting out a 30-year plan to expand ties and to institutionalize relations. As Ji Da-gyum wrote for The Korea Herald, one of the central motivations for the Seoul Declaration is to turn existing political commitment “into a more durable institutional framework.” Under that emerging framework leaders-level summits are expected biennially, with the next envisioned for 2028 in Kazakhstan.

articles.title: What Do Taiwan’s People Think About Its Annual Military Exercises?
articles.full_text:
Taiwan’s Han Kuang exercises are winning public approval, despite the growing impact on civilians. Understanding is another matter.
Taiwanese soldiers during the 2026 Han Kuang exercises, Aug. 8, 2026.
Taiwan’s annual Han Kuang military exercises were difficult for ordinary citizens to ignore this year. Mobile internet was deliberately slowed for 30 minutes to simulate wartime communications disruptions. Troops barricaded Guangfu Bridge, a key route connecting New Taipei City with the capital, setting up metal barriers and barbed wire as they rehearsed stopping enemy forces from advancing into Taipei. Hospitals also practiced moving medical operations underground as part of exercises designed to keep essential services running during a conflict. These scenes showed how Taiwan’s preparations for a possible war are moving beyond conventional military exercises and increasingly into the spaces of everyday civilian life.
The shift reflects a broader change in Taiwan’s approach to defense. This year’s Han Kuang exercises placed greater emphasis on realistic wartime scenarios while more closely integrating military training with urban resilience exercises. Preparing for a potential conflict is increasingly not only a task for the armed forces, but also a challenge involving civilian infrastructure, local governments, reservists, and ordinary citizens. But as Taiwan brings society more directly into its defense preparations, a basic question becomes more important: What do Taiwanese themselves make of the country’s most important annual military exercise?
To answer this question, the Institute for National Defense and Security Research (INDSR) commissioned a nationwide telephone survey shortly after this year’s exercises. Conducted by National Chengchi University’s Election Study Center from August 20 to 24, the survey interviewed 1,215 adults across Taiwan. Public satisfaction with the Han Kuang exercises reached its highest level in our survey series, yet most respondents said they knew relatively little about what the exercises actually involved. The findings suggest that as Taiwan expands whole-of-society defense, public approval and public understanding should not be treated as the same thing.
Public satisfaction with the Han Kuang exercises reached 60 percent this year, the highest level in our survey series. As shown in the chart below, satisfaction had generally hovered around 50 percent in previous surveys. It stood at 51.9 percent in 2021 and 53.6 percent in 2022, before falling to 45.5 percent in 2023. Satisfaction recovered to 51.3 percent in 2025 (there was no comparable survey in 2024) and rose further this year. The longer-term pattern has therefore fluctuated rather than followed a steady upward trend, but the 2026 result is noticeably higher than the levels recorded in previous surveys.
The figure also shows another shift. The share of respondents who did not offer a clear evaluation of the exercises – whether they chose now to answer or were unaware of the exercises at all – fell from 36.7 percent in 2021 to 25.3 percent in 2026, the lowest level in our survey series, although the decline was not consistent across years. Among those who reached the satisfaction question this year, about three-quarters expressed either a positive or negative view of the exercises. 
These comparisons require some caution because the screening questions and skip patterns were not identical across survey waves. More importantly, being able to evaluate the exercises does not necessarily mean understanding them better. When we asked respondents directly how well they understood the Han Kuang exercises, the results told a different story.
Only 2.3 percent of respondents said they understood them very well and 22.6 percent somewhat well. By comparison, 46.1 percent said they did not understand the exercises very well, while another 26.4 percent said they did not understand them at all. In other words, nearly three-quarters of respondents described their understanding of the exercises as limited.
These findings do not necessarily contradict the relatively high level of satisfaction with this year’s exercises. People can form an overall impression of Han Kuang through news coverage, social media, or the activities they encounter in daily life without knowing in detail what individual drills are designed to test. Satisfaction captures how people evaluate the exercises, but it tells us less about how well they understand their purpose. 
As Taiwan places greater emphasis on whole-of-society defense, the distance between approval and understanding becomes harder to ignore. Citizens are no longer simply an audience observing how well the military performs. They are increasingly expected to understand how society would function under crisis conditions and how civilian preparedness connects to national defense. That makes public understanding more consequential than it was when military exercises were viewed mainly as the work of the armed forces.
Satisfaction, understanding, and preparedness are therefore related but distinct. A citizen can support the Han Kuang exercises without knowing what they are intended to test or how they fit into Taiwan’s broader defense planning. Such support is still valuable. It gives the exercises public legitimacy and suggests that many people see value in continued preparation. But support alone does not tell us whether citizens are better prepared to interpret official instructions, understand disruptions during a crisis, or recognize their own responsibilities. 
Of course, not every citizen needs detailed knowledge of military operations. What is needed is a more basic level of understanding. People should know what the exercises are trying to prepare for, why civilian participation is necessary, and how individual drills connect to the wider goal of national resilience. Public communication should therefore do more than make Han Kuang visible. It should help citizens make sense of what they are seeing. 
For Taiwan, the next challenge is not simply getting citizens to watch Han Kuang, but helping them understand what they are watching and why it matters.

articles.title: The Challenges of Finding Political Treasure in Chinese Overseas Ports
articles.full_text:
When it comes to Chinese overseas port projects, negative economic externalities may coexist with positive ones.
China’s recent 8th Silk Road Maritime International Cooperation Forum kept the spotlight on Chinese overseas ports, a subject of continuing attention in the news, among think tanks, and in scholarly circles. Although the bulk of commentary emphasizes a geopolitical angle, others devote attention to the economic value of China’s overseas ports presence, especially in countries that have welcomed Chinese investors, contractors, and terminal operators. Among other gains, they expect greater connectivity, employment growth, and shifts to higher value-added activities.  For its part, China touts economic returns from its ports such as higher transport volumes, increased exports, and workforce development in places like Egypt.
The actual economic impact flowing from China’s port participation is not just a domestic or international economic issue. It is a domestic and international political issue and thus needs thoughtful consideration. Discussing this impact is the purpose of this piece, the third in a four-part series on China’s footprint in overseas ports. The first part examined China and Chinese companies’ sundry motives, their footprint, and storms about their presence. The second delved at length into the hopes and fears of host countries, third-parties like the United States, and others with respect to “Chinese” ports’ speculated positive and negative outcomes.
At the most basic level, host countries envision that their ports will improve due to the new berths, expanded terminals, better cranes, deeper ports, enhanced port infrastructure, and modernized IT systems flowing from Chinese involvement. Such changes have featured in Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) and European ports ranging from Balboa and Cristobal (Panama) to Zeebrugge (Belgium) as well as Southeast and South Asian ports such as Kyaukphyu Made Island (Myanmar) and Mongla (Bangladesh). Port improvements, in turn, will enable them to handle bigger ships, larger cargo volumes, and different vessel types. All of this will boost port earnings, tax revenues, and local port business activities. Furthermore, there will be job creation. 
Aside from this, linked infrastructure improvements should spur local economic activity and amplify the benefits of proximate special economic zones (SEZs). SEZs are a regular feature of China’s ports’ footprint and, in fact, may be their most prominent one as seen in Middle Eastern countries such as the United Arab Emirates. Beyond the above, host countries anticipate export growth, greater inward foreign direct investment (FDI) flows, and richer integration with global networks.
Dredging through the data, an analysis of China’s footprint in 20 ports in Europe and the LAC determined Chinese investment indeed led to, among other things, new, bigger, or modernized quays, terminals, and intermodal transportation links. This, in turn, boosted capacity, turnaround times, and efficiency. More than two-thirds of ports where data was available showed improved port performance. Likewise, more than two-thirds of ports, witnessed increased connectivity. On top of this, the analysis uncovered that Chinese ports directly created or preserved hundreds and even thousands of jobs. Some ports became notable revenue and tax generators. 
A later study of China’s participation in numerous ports in Southeast and South Asia identified similar, positive outcomes. Ports improvements in countries like Bangladesh, Myanmar, and the Philippines were commonplace and these fueled increased capacity, improved turnaround times, higher rankings, local development, and more. Job creation also followed, though specifics were lacking. Unlike the European and LAC cases, this study did not uncover major revenue or tax boosts. There was almost no evidence of technology transfer, blossoming SEZs, or dramatically positive trade pattern changes in the four regions.
Not highlighted above, but well covered in the aforementioned analyses, is the diversity of China’s participation in overseas ports, which entails investing, contracting, terminal operations, sales, and services. In addition, there are notable variations in Chinese project types ranging from dredging to terminal modernization to deep-water port construction. Further muddying the waters is the fact that many projects, once underway, do not reflect their original designs. For instance, in Southeast and South Asia, for instance, this was true in 47 percent of studied cases. Reasons include local port defects, domestic politics, host country financial limits, the capabilities of the Chinese investor/contractor, and opposition by third parties like Japan. Whatever the cause, the disconnect between vision and reality means that many port projects are not yielding benefits nor changing port features and outputs in transformative ways. 
It is important to mention that China’s ports presence may be associated with negative outcomes, too. These may include the crowding out of local maritime firms, the loss of jobs at ports, accelerated deindustrialization, greater trade imbalances, and dependence on Chinese shipping networks.
The preceding highlights three key points. First, Chinese port involvement does not always come to fruition and, even if does, deliverables may not match desires. Second, China’s ports participation frequently yields benefits at the level of ports, but not necessarily at the local, regional, or national levels. Third, negative economic externalities may coexist with positive ones. 
Given these points, commentators need to anchor their conclusions with a serious assessment of the net benefit of China’s ports footprint, a point I have made regarding Chinese FDI more generally. Contrary to expectations, the net return actually may lead to anti-port sentiments in host countries that impede project initiation, development, and results, limit closer relations between host countries and China, or prevent adverse third-party foreign policy effects. Presuming predetermined outcomes is inadvisable.
The next part in this series will ponder the political and military risks associated with China’s involvement in overseas ports.

articles.title: The New Delhi BRICS Summit Sends Powerful Messages to America
articles.full_text:
However determined Western governments may be to turn Russia and Iran into pariah states, much of the Global South rejects their isolation.
Russian President Vladimir Putin, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and China President Xi Jinping join hands at the 18th BRICS summit at New Delhi, India, Sept. 12, 2026.
India hosted the 18th BRICS Summit with considerable success and impact. This year’s summit generated consensus on several major issues that concern not only BRICS members but also much of the world beyond the U.S.-dominated West.
In the wake of this summit, one can legitimately argue that BRICS is emerging as a formidable grouping capable of challenging the global hegemony of the United States and the G7. More importantly, it is evolving into a global platform that can help its members move, as India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi put it, from being “rule takers” to becoming “rule makers.”
India achieved something that had seemed nearly impossible only a few months ago: securing the unanimous endorsement of a joint declaration by all BRICS nations. At the May meeting of BRICS foreign ministers, deep internal disagreements — particularly between India, which was reluctant to condemn Israel and the United States, and other members that sought such condemnation over the Israeli-U.S. attacks on Iran — prevented consensus. A separate dispute between the UAE and Iran over the wording of the document ultimately scuttled the proposed joint declaration, forcing the chair to issue only a summary of the discussions.
That failure highlighted the divisions within BRICS and raised serious questions about whether it could ever become a cohesive grouping. Its members include countries that are strategic rivals, such as India and China, as well as states directly at war with one another, such as the UAE and Iran. Yet India’s Ministry of External Affairs and its BRICS sherpas worked diligently to produce a draft acceptable to every member. All sides made significant compromises to reach consensus.
The resulting declaration sends a powerful signal: a united BRICS is prepared to engage with and reshape the global order — not by dismantling it, but by preserving its liberal foundations. This creates a striking reversal in global politics. The United States, which underwrote the liberal international order for more than seven decades, now appears determined to weaken it, tarnish its legitimacy, undermine core institutions such as the ICC and the ICJ, and render the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) increasingly irrelevant.
Contrary to the perception that BRICS seeks to challenge the U.S.-led global order, it is essentially pursuing a course correction. It seeks to ensure that the liberal order and its underlying principles are not diminished by double standards and unilateral actions, particularly those of the United States. BRICS is thus positioning itself as a defender of the fundamental principles upon which that order rests: state sovereignty, international law, international norms, and, above all, mutual respect among nations.
The New Delhi Declaration was remarkable and surprising in several respects. It remained consistent with the broad narrative advanced by India: that BRICS is not anti-American, anti-Western, or directed against any particular country. Rather, BRICS is an endeavor by states to come together to address common challenges and pursue mutually shared interests. What was particularly remarkable, however, was India’s ability to secure consensus on several highly contentious issues.
Four major features of the declaration deserve particular attention.
First, notwithstanding its carefully calibrated rhetoric, the declaration was strongly critical of U.S. trade and sanctions practices. It condemned unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures that distort trade and violate WTO rules. It also denounced unilateral economic and secondary sanctions imposed outside the authority of the UNSC, characterizing such measures as contrary to international law and harmful to the development, health, and food security of affected populations, particularly in the Global South (paragraphs 21–22).
Second, each of the three major BRICS powers — China, Russia, and India — managed to incorporate its particular priorities into the declaration. China secured a strong condemnation of unilateral sanctions, many of which are directed against it. Even sanctions targeting Iran indirectly affect China because it is the principal purchaser of Iranian oil. Russia, too, secured what it wanted: Ukraine was omitted. Far from criticizing Russia, the declaration remained entirely silent about the Ukraine war and its effects on global supply chains and the international order.
India, meanwhile, obtained the unified BRICS position it has consistently sought against cross-border terrorism, terrorist financing, and safe havens for terrorist groups (paragraph 40). The declaration condemns the April 22, 2025, terrorist attack in Jammu and Kashmir, in which 26 people were killed, and explicitly calls for combating the cross-border movement of terrorists, terrorism financing, and terrorist safe havens. Although the paragraph does not mention Pakistan, it clearly advances, legitimizes, and showcases India’s concerns about its problematic neighbor and its policies aimed at destabilizing Kashmir through cross-border terrorism.
Third, perhaps the most astonishing feature of the declaration was its treatment of the war against Iran (paragraphs 28–29). The document protects the United States and Israel to some extent by declining to name them, but its criticism of their attacks on Iran is nevertheless unmistakable. It expresses concern about escalating tensions in West Asia, stresses the protection of civilian infrastructure and the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states, and condemns deliberate attacks on peaceful nuclear facilities operating under full IAEA safeguards as violations of international law. The declaration therefore affirms the protected status of Iran’s peaceful nuclear infrastructure and establishes that attacks against it are illegal, while offering no comparable criticism of Iran’s attacks on its Gulf neighbors.
Finally, the declaration’s extensive treatment of Palestine, followed by its discussion of Lebanon, constitutes a profound indictment of Israel even when Israel is not always explicitly named. It condemns forced displacement, starvation as a method of warfare, attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, and the obstruction of humanitarian assistance. It reaffirms the Palestinians’ rights to self-determination and return, supports full Palestinian membership in the United Nations, and reiterates its commitment to a sovereign Palestinian state within the internationally recognized 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital (paragraphs 30–34). It then condemns violations of Lebanon’s sovereignty, calls explicitly on Israel to withdraw from occupied Lebanese territory, and denounces attacks against UNIFIL personnel and installations (paragraphs 35–36).
